Identity

Pareto Talent — Identity

  • Company: Pareto Talent — US LLC, Scottsdale, Arizona (America/Phoenix, UTC-7, no daylight saving)
  • Founded: 2023, by kasim-aslam and ivan-bunin after they sold Solutions 8 (October 2022). $1M+ revenue in year 1, on referrals alone, zero paid ads
  • What it does: finds, trains, places and supports elite full-time Right Hands (Executive Assistants) from Latin America for 7–8-figure US founders — “AI-Powered Right Hands” trained 40+ hours on the AI stack (Claude, ChatGPT, Canva, CapCut, N8N, Lovable, Operator AI)
  • Model: find → train (free 10-day Bootcamp) → place (up to 3 candidates, matched in 24h, reviewed by Kasim) → support (Success Manager, community, lifetime replacement)

  • Money: candidates start at $1,000/month (USD, no cap); founders pay $3,000/month annual + $3,000 one-time placement fee. Three guarantees: Freedom 40, Matching, Lifetime Replacement
  • Culture: no screen monitoring ever · 20 days PTO (1.7/month accrual) · “hire for will, train for skill” · people are miracles, not commodities

Jargon

Jargon & Glossary

Pareto Talent core terms

  • EA / Right Hand — the full-time executive assistant placed with a founder (“Right Hand” = strategic, not task-taker)
  • The Bootcamp — free 10-day live training (2 h/day + homework) that feeds the talent pool; final project decides graduation
  • Pareto Talent Framework — the 7-step hiring system from the-hire-book: clarify principles → job posting → distribution → filter the stack → tryouts → interviews → onboard
  • Success Pillars — compensation, community, purpose, freedom, growth (retention levers)
  • Hiring Regions — SE Asia, South Asia, LATAM, Eastern Europe, North Africa & Middle East, Canada
  • Wall of Love — testimonial page organized by tenure (30/90/365 days): wall-of-love
  • Matching Call — the founder’s sales call after the funnel video; ends with 3 hand-picked profiles in 24 hours
  • PI Behavioral Assessment — personality profiling used for founder–EA compatibility
  • AI-Powered Right Hand — current positioning; 40+ hrs AI-stack training, tool subscriptions covered

Offer components (founder side)

  • Freedom 40 Guarantee — reclaim 10+ hrs/week in the first phase or [terms on the site]
  • Matching Guarantee — no contract until the founder hires one of the presented candidates
  • Lifetime Replacement — the EA can always be swapped; same guarantee protects EAs via the handbook
  • Delegation Mastermind — weekly calls with Kasim + ~100 founders; the 7 Laws of Delegation
  • Talent Success Manager — runs the founder’s HR function for the placed EA
  • Second Brain OS — Pareto’s own offer component: decisions, SOPs, vendors, meeting notes in one system (the reason this vault exists, effectively)

Money & policy

  • $1,000/month starting salary (USD, Wise/Payoneer) · 20 days PTO accrued 1.7/month · no screen monitoring ever · $100/month subscriptions covered

Companies

Pareto Talent

Pareto Talent

US LLC headquartered in Scottsdale, Arizona (MST — Arizona does not observe daylight saving time). Co-founded by kasim-aslam and ivan-bunin after they sold Solutions 8 in October 2022. The company launched in 2023 and cleared $1M+ in its first year on referrals alone (public site).

The model

Find → train → place → support: 1. Find — applicants go through a screening funnel (application with filters, live bootcamp). 2. Train — free 10-day live Bootcamp, 2 h/day + daily homework. See pareto-bootcamp. 3. Place — graduates join the talent pool; Pareto matches them with pre-vetted US entrepreneurs and presents up to 3 candidates per role. 4. Support — client success managers, weekly trainings, community, lifetime replacement guarantee.

The hiring philosophy behind all of this is written up in the-hire-book (pareto-talent-framework).

Key numbers (BC7 era, late 2026)

  • 100+ founders actively working with placed EAs; 250+ EA community members.
  • ~3,000 people graduated across 7 bootcamps; 2M+ people in Argentina saw their ads.
  • Lifetime funnel: 35,000+ applicants → 2,000+ finished the bootcamp → ~350 accepted into Pareto Talent.
  • Last cohort: 10,000 applications → 700 accepted → 247 finished final project → 118 accepted.
  • BC7: 7,000+ applications, ~885 approved, ~800 expected live.
  • Public site (Oct 2026): 100+ founders paired, 93% retention at 12 months, 4.9★ average, zero ad spend (all word-of-mouth), 650+ pre-vetted candidates on file — ~1 in 1,000 applicants makes it in.

Compensation & policies

  • Starting salary $1,000/month full-time (higher with relevant experience: medical background, languages, dev skills, etc.). Paid in USD via Payoneer/Wise — no currency lock-in.
  • 20 days PTO per year, accrued at 1.7 days/month, use-it-or-lose-it (same policy Kasim writes into client contracts in the book).
  • No screen monitoring or screenshots — trust-based, self-managed.
  • Up to $100/month in tool subscriptions covered; equipment support (MacBooks) after ~90 days placed; entrepreneur covers health costs.
  • EA of the Month / EA of the Year awards; lifetime replacement guarantee (works both ways — replaced if not a fit, as long as compliant with the handbook).
  • Entrepreneurs are vetted too: intake process, onboarding, personality tests before they ever interview a right hand.

Offer to founders (public pricing, Oct 2026)

  • $3,000/month on the annual plan + one-time $3,000 placement fee; no contract until you hire (Matching Guarantee). Positioning: AI-Powered Right Hand — 40+ hrs of AI-stack training (Claude, ChatGPT, Canva, CapCut, N8N, Lovable, Operator AI), tool subscriptions covered by Pareto.
  • The stack of 7: the Right Hand itself · Delegation Mastermind (weekly calls with Kasim + ~100 founders) · Right Hand community (250+) · 10-day AI Bootcamp + 104 trainings/yr · three guarantees (Freedom 40, Matching, Lifetime Replacement) · Pareto Second Brain OS (SOPs, decisions, vendors in one system) · Talent Success Manager (runs the founder’s whole HR function).
  • Process: PI behavioral assessment → role alignment → meet the top 3 → 30-day integration with a Success Manager.

Ecosystem

  • Architects.com — sister company placing technical talent.
  • Community: 70+ weekly trainings recorded, 35+ Udemy courses included, offline events (Buenos Aires rooftop 2026, Bogotá 2025), birthday gifts, merch.
  • Ivan relocated to Montevideo, Uruguay in 2026 to be close to the LATAM talent base.

Ivan Bunin

Ivan Bunin

Co-founder of pareto-talent, bootcamp lead instructor, co-author of the-hire-book. Kasim’s third EA — the one who became CTO and then business partner (the Growth pillar case study from the book).

Path

  • Started freelancing at 16 (graphic design, logos, dropshipping), switching entrepreneurs every few months at $400–600/month while at university.
  • 2018: applied to an EA job at Kasim’s small agency (6 people, Arizona). Asked for $1,000, was offered $1,200/month — first job that didn’t feel like a scam.
  • Grew EA → technical team lead → CTO as the agency scaled to 60 people (Solutions 8). Ran the due diligence and data room for the 2022 sale, then co-launched Pareto Talent with Kasim.
  • Based in Montevideo, Uruguay (since ~2026); previously 3 years in the US, before that Europe.

What he teaches / operates

  • Context over prompts — AI output is only as good as the context you feed it (“trash in, trash out”). Everything is context: call recordings, YouTube transcripts, Drive files, scraped sites, email threads.
  • Marries one tool (claude) instead of chasing every new model.
  • Second brains in Obsidian (~6,000 markdown docs feeding AI).
  • Dictation over typing (Whisperflow) — dictates context naturally.
  • EA operations: shortwave for inbox, inbox zero, calendar Tetris, security hygiene (2FA, passkeys, Bitwarden/Keychain), booking calendars, time zones.

Recurring sayings

  • “You are not hired to answer emails — you’re hired to close the loops.”
  • “Working ON the business, not IN the business.”
  • “You’re the context source: sit down with AI, answer 20 questions, and the one-pager you get back becomes context you never have to repeat.”

Danish Ashrafi And Collin Schmelebeck

Case studies: Danish Ashrafi & Collin Schmelebeck

Two proof points for “support side hustles and growth instead of retaining” (success-pillars).

Danish Ashrafi

  • “Digital hacker” who could solve just about any problem. His freelance business grew faster than the role Kasim had for him, so he struck out on his own.
  • Kasim became one of his regular clients and referred people to him constantly.
  • Danish later emailed about an opportunity bigger than he could handle → Kasim got cc’d on an email with Jay Abraham’s CMO — one of the biggest referral opportunities of his life came from a Pakistan-based freelancer he used to employ.

Collin Schmelebeck

  • Now one of the biggest names in Google Ads. Before Twitter fame, he worked for Kasim for 2 years while already building his freelance business — one of the best employees he ever had. Left on great terms: tons of notice, trained his replacement, stayed available.
  • Collin wanted a boutique, so he took the difficult clients Solutions 8 didn’t want → Kasim monetized dead leads via referral fees. Collin sent clients back and coached Kasim on growing his Twitter — following doubled in months.
  • “What if I’d tried to retain Collin? I probably wouldn’t have hired him at all — and if I had, I would’ve forced him to build his business in secret.”

Broader pattern: former employees hired Kasim’s agency, booked him speaking gigs and podcasts, offered him equity. Be the incubator and it flows back.

Media & Learning

Hiring Regions

Hiring Regions

Bonus chapter of the-hire-book. Framed by the authors as context, not a rulebook — broad generalizations to bridge cultural gaps, every hire is an individual. Deeper tool: Hofstede’s Five Dimensions of Culture — theculturefactor.com.

Southeast Asia (Philippines, Vietnam, Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia)

  • Philippines is the classic outsourcing hub — availability tightening as Western companies open offices; consider widening the geofence.
  • Salary: budget the “13th month” (extra month’s salary at year end — a big deal around the holidays).
  • Conflict style: famously conflict-averse (Pakikisama — keeping the peace). “Filipinos view Americans the way Americans view Germans.” They may suffer in silence — check in often, listen carefully (the Angelia story: workload tripled, burned out quietly).
  • Power: traditional environments expect directions followed exactly; creativity must be earned and made safe.
  • Family: deeply family-oriented, income shared with extended family — non-cash rewards (gifts) carry extra meaning.

South Asia (India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Nepal)

  • “Jugaad mentality” — scrappy, resourceful problem-solving; sometimes quick fixes not built for the long haul. Thrive with structure + room to innovate.
  • Time is fluid; deadlines are guidelines — set clear expectations, build in buffers, check in early and often.
  • Formal, diplomatic in writing; more relaxed live. Indirect “no”: “I’ll try”, “Inshallah” ≠ firm commitment. Public correction shames; public praise carries real weight.
  • Hierarchy runs deep; seniority respected; initiative needs explicit permission until you make experimentation safe.
  • Family commitments come first (extended leave for weddings/religious holidays; India has huge holiday counts) — many make up hours and adapt to US/EU time zones; graveyard shifts are culturally normalized.

Latin America (Argentina, Mexico, Colombia, Brazil, Nicaragua)

  • Not a monolith. Common thread: trust is earned, deeply — personal and professional.
  • Outgoing, collaborative, entrepreneurial; “work to live” — strong ethic, but job titles don’t define identity. Don’t mistake adaptability (from economic turmoil) for disengagement. “LATAM time” exists, but strict-punctuality roles are handled fine when expectations are explicit.
  • Money motivates — but when a financial goal is hit, some “peace out”; stretch bonuses over time instead of lump sums. Flexibility sometimes outranks salary. Argentina: Aguinaldo (13th salary) split July + December, standard compensation.
  • Warm, expressive communication; Argentinians notably polite/formal. Corporate jargon and rigid systems feel impersonal. Remote work can feel isolating — Slack channels, huddles, low-stakes fun help.
  • Relaxed hierarchy; comfortable with leadership; team loyalty matters. Personal time guarded — respect it for retention.
  • Recap: energy, loyalty, US time-zone alignment, familiar communication. Slightly harder for niche technical skills vs Asia; ease of collaboration makes up for it.

Eastern Europe (Ukraine, Poland, Romania, Hungary, Czech Republic)

  • Resilient, skilled, proud of their work; tough, pragmatic, committed to excellence. If they commit, they deliver; if unsure, they won’t say yes. Expect friction with flexible-timeline cultures unless bridged upfront.
  • Salaries higher than Asia — less arbitrage, high quality. Stability wins loyalty; once secure, they take real ownership. Rule-followers who value fairness and own their mistakes.
  • Famously direct — they want the reasoning behind decisions, and follow competent leaders with serious buy-in. Sense incompetence → quiet disengagement, no drama. Praise and feedback must be specific and actionable; fluff gets challenged. Practicality beats vision statements.
  • Hierarchy is conditional — respect is earned, titles don’t cut it.
  • Family duty runs deep; appreciate vacation but may not take it unless encouraged.

North Africa & The Middle East (Egypt, Morocco, Tunisia, Turkey)

  • Incredibly resilient under pressure; community rallies in crisis.
  • Time flexible unless urgency is established — set and reinforce expectations early.
  • Money talks (extended-family support), bonuses and performance incentives deeply appreciated; public recognition matters if authentic and from someone respected. Job security is a major driver.
  • Colorful communication — metaphor, hyperbole, emotion; read between the lines. Excellent negotiators (great for sales/client-facing) but may overpromise — build in checks.
  • Saving face: give feedback privately, with clear affirmation. Early “cover your ass” behaviors are self-preservation, not low confidence — they fade as trust grows.
  • Relationships run the show; leaders are seen as protectors, not delegators-and-disappearers. Family stretches to third/fourth cousins — work and life integrate rather than compartmentalize.

Bonus: Canada

  • Underrated “outsourcing” destination: strong cultural alignment with the US, no major time-zone or language friction, favorable exchange rate ($50K USD ≈ $70K CAD). Toronto/Vancouver are pricey; Edmonton/Calgary are the sweet spot. Universal healthcare simplifies things.
  • Polite, reserved; conflict handled diplomatically (can read as indirect). Consensus-leaning, slightly bureaucratic — many who’d found in the US choose stable employment instead, so the pool of skilled, loyal professionals is deep. Work-life balance baked in; consistency and long-term loyalty.

Pareto Talent Framework

The Pareto Talent Framework

7-step hiring process from the-hire-book. It looks backwards on purpose: instead of interviewing first, it filters with flytraps and paid trial work before any interview, so you only interview people already proven to do the job. Nothing is sacred — chop it up per role.

Step Note One-liner
1 step-1-clarify-your-core-principles Align beliefs before hiring anything
2 step-2-create-a-job-posting The posting is a sales letter full of flytraps
3 step-3-plan-your-distribution-strategy Pick the pool (language, infra, skills, time, culture), then post wide
4 step-4-filter-the-stack Binary filter on instructions, then qualitative filter
5 step-5-run-the-tryouts Skip first interviews — pay everyone a 2-hour trial project
6 step-6-conduct-the-interviews Final filter: confirm what the trial already showed
7 step-7-onboard-for-success First 90 days = launch sequence

Supporting concepts: - success-pillars — what makes winners want to work for you - hiring-regions — where to hire and what to expect culturally - Target funnel math: thousands of applicants → 5–10 viable per hire → 3–5 finalists after trials → 1 hire

Media & Learning

Principle 1 Empathize

Principle 1 — Empathize

The foundational principle: place yourself in the prospect’s shoes. People buy feelings, not products — purchasing decisions are psychological, not logical.

Building an Avatar

Your Avatar is a single, idealized individual, not a target demographic. Questions: average day, free time, goals, values, challenges, pain points, where they get information, trusted media, influencers, when/how they engage content, peer group, associations, education, worries, responsibilities, turn-offs. Never done building — keep editing; split or add Avatars as segments emerge. Anecdotal evidence is fine (this data exists nowhere else) — validate and revisit later. - Dr. Mike vs Dr. Jenny (same “demographic”, opposite messaging): Mike, early 50s, wants to transition out, delegates, needs revenue-tied efficiency. Jenny, early 30s, hands-on, limited budget/big ideas, starting from zero, wants cutting edge.

Empathy applied

  • Capture earlier in the funnel = cheaper leads + marketing in a silo (no competitors on screen): website-rebuild buyers search “how to fix a hacked website” long before “best website design company Phoenix”. Trade-off: higher-funnel leads are cheaper but diluted and slower to nurture.
  • B2B/B2C is dead — it’s B2P (business to person). You sell to the engineer/project manager/buyer, not the company. Some “stacked” Avatars (medical equipment: doctor + administrator). P2P: people buy from people; brand the person when possible.
  • Who are you serving? The client’s prospect, not the client, not your CEO’s wishes, and not the data (iPad giveaways = unsegmented disgruntled lists; a courier’s free month of deliveries pulled ravenous relevant attention).

The funnel

  • Old: Awareness → Interest → Consideration → Intent → Evaluation → Purchase, with marketing owning the top three.
  • New: marketing owns the whole thing, extended post-purchase: + Service, Engagement, Renewal, Ascension. Onboarding, reviews, referrals, satisfaction surveys, retention and ascension campaigns are digital marketing.
  • Find the existing funnel — people travel one with or without you. Replicate the logical path; break norms only with a value-added purpose (flat-fee Salesforce integration bidding instead of hourly).

Content + Context

Same content, different context = different approach. Ask: Where am I approaching them? Am I a destination (search intent — speak value directly) or a distraction (feed-scroll — engage, nurture longer)? How do they expect to be approached (forum etiquette; LinkedIn InMail with a free explainer video + guest blog offer = yes)? What voice fits the conduit (YouTube ≠ Snapchat ≠ email)? What do they already know? What baggage do they carry (dentists are pre-burned on marketing — never ignore it)? What misconceptions (business consultants are oversold on digital marketing)?

Narrative

People think in stories; narrative creates empathic reciprocity. A well-built funnel is a story ending in Client → advocate. Continuity is the discipline: subject line → email copy → CTA → destination must align (no clickbait); ad → landing page → button → thank-you page → follow-up must keep one promise chain; and deliver the promise — fulfillment is part of marketing.

Intuitive decisions, data-driven adjustments

Empathy first, then test. Data only measures what’s been tried — 100% data-driven = 100% derivative. But interrogate the why behind results (“sell my house” outsold “sell my home” — psychological attachment). Abdicating decisions to data makes you worth less than a computer.

Understanding a network

Every network has a culture (Facebook = staying current, Instagram = dreaming; Reddit fury; LinkedIn’s monetized manners). Don’t cascade identical posts everywhere; learn the room before entering the conversation — like visiting someone’s home.

Do this

Keep a journal as your Avatar · assign an Avatar advocate on every campaign · be your Avatar’s best friend · be your Avatar.

Media & Learning

Principle 2 Be The First And Last To Give Value

Principle 2 — Be the First (and Last) to Give Value

Transactional relationships (vending machines, lead-magnet-for-email swaps) have no quantifiable future. The value-first principle: you always provide value first, without contingency — no “now you owe me”.

Deposits and withdrawals

Ryan Deiss’s bank-account analogy: every relationship is an account. Withdrawals aren’t just money — asking for time, feedback, referrals, testimonials all withdraw. Deposits must always exceed withdrawals, and you should be first and last to deposit. Giving without expectation builds the one thing that starts every relationship: trust.

Lockstep value (the ascension model)

The Spartacus CPA example, step by step: 1. Full actionable blog post, free, no gate (deposit) — not a synopsis with the how-to held hostage for an email. 2. Soft CTA inside the content: an Excel worksheet implementing the article (a supplement, not a requirement for value). 3. Deliver worksheet + a free video training course on using it — over-delivery trains the neuro-association “he always over-delivers”. 4. Engagement emails → the ask: a $497 flat-fee audit (25-point proprietary audit, normally four-to-five figures) with nothing held back and a 100% money-back guarantee. First purchase acclimates the prospect to spending — “approved vendor” positioning — and the audit is paid discovery for future services. Pixel engaged users and remarket the next value step throughout their browsing.

Marketing in a silo

Value-first pulls users out of the buying cycle: they stop searching, so you qualify them against your offer instead of differentiating against competitors. Nutritionist case study: the free consult was commoditized (everyone offered it, cost-prohibitive to scale) → front-loaded high-value “how-to” content, then charged for the consult with a 3-tier guarantee (nothing held back · consult fee credited toward further services · 100% refund if value doesn’t exceed price). Fewer leads, 2x+ qualified leads, scalable. Caution: a silo must stay defensible if the prospect peeks outside. Amplify value up to a price you can justify — never mask commoditization.

If you can’t start with more value, end with it

Dentist example (saturated market, loss-leader $39 specials): start a timeline + goals narrative at the first visit — periodontal scores, checklist for the bathroom mirror, segmented email nurture with custom goal snippets, then a free 3-month checkup instead of six. The patient is now in a story they won’t abandon. Harder than front-loading, but it works.

Social proof > brand recognition

What people say about your brand outweighs whether they recognize it (the whole Google algorithm is peer review). Collect it: end-of-video asks, “be featured in our next blast — tell us how we helped you”. Manage the negative: automated post-service yes/no email — “no” routes to a make-it-right form for the department manager, “yes” routes to a thank-you + testimonial request across networks. Keep negative reviews visible against a forgiving backdrop of positives.

The value of valuable content

Content for content’s sake is the scourge of the internet. Standard: 10x content (Rand Fishkin). Treat your content like a paid subscription publication — you are paid for it, in attention (Gary Vaynerchuk: he day-trades attention). Attention can beat engagement: Company A has the client, Company B has the Avatar’s focused attention — B wins long-term. Whatever your business, you’re now also in the content business. Outsource creation, never thought leadership (pass-down routines: commute videos, voice notes; a prioritized topic list with visibility; repurpose everything — article → infographic → slides → video).

The after-value value

Clients at the “end of the line” are your gold mine: they trust you most and will tell you what to build next. Keep depositing: single-question surveys, referral/testimonial asks, training content (cabinet-stocking videos, rug-rotation reminders with approved vendors, WordPress-update emails with how-to videos). Caution on affiliate blasts: “Is this providing more value, or monetizing them one last time?”

Principle 3 Learn Apply And Innovate

Principle 3 — Learn, Apply & Innovate

A three-part sequence; the parts can’t stand alone. Digital marketing is a lifestyle, not a job — if constant learning doesn’t resonate, re-examine the fit.

Learn

  • Learn like a philosophy student, not a technician: what’s available, how/why/when to use it, whom it serves, how it’s changing. You’re the quarterback, not the lawn mower — you don’t need to press every button, you need to know when it should be pressed and who should press it. (If you also wear a technician hat, stay sharp there too.)
  • Cadence: something small daily (~10 min), medium weekly (~1 h), large monthly (~4 h) — Kasim: one blog/day, one white paper/week, one book/month. Diversify sources; the best content often comes from obscure places, not the best promoters.
  • Teach to learn: fact-check harder when someone will challenge you. Sprint-blogging (write everything, delete nothing, edit at the end) cements retention.

Sources

  • Thought leaders (summarizers vs prognosticators — temper the un-vetted futurists), content networks (verify author credibility), competitors both big and small (small agencies and solo consultants invent the disruptive tactics), and your clients (learn everything about their offer — but you’re the expert on marketing; “my customers aren’t on Facebook” is often wrong).
  • SME ≠ decision maker: the office manager isn’t the dentist, the CMO’s assertions can contradict his sales staff. Sniff out the true source, protect the client from themselves, always ask “why?” to find where beliefs were formed.

Marketing is learning

80% of ads fail — embrace “fail early, fail often”, but never leave failure unexamined; find the point of failure. Also learn from successes (repeatedly making the same correction = a process problem).

Apply

Build a system: the monthly plan meeting — everyone owns their vertical, brings improvement ideas, implications are discussed, action items assigned, one campaign chosen as the test, reviewed at the next monthly plan. No knee-jerk rewrites from a guru video.

Romantics make bad digital marketers

Don’t get attached: Kasim dislikes Facebook and Bing yet tests Bing with every client and let Facebook take half the PPC business. Don’t chase “X is dead” headlines either — don’t let what works now distract from tomorrow, and don’t abandon what works because of a picket sign. Livelihoods shouldn’t rest on any single entity (Rome fell; Google may too).

Plausible deniability is a learning blocker

Some avoid learning so they can keep doing it the old way “innocently”. There is no plausible deniability in this field. An antiquated business model is usually an upsell opportunity in disguise.

Innovate

  • Experimentation may be 5% of the work and 90% of the growth. Innovate the last 5–10% of proven campaigns; don’t wildcat brand-new strategy.
  • Always be testing — one variable at a time, simple identifiable differences, test to tedium, then restart with new variables.
  • Fail good: make an assumption → define the control group → build the test environment → run and monitor → gather and evaluate data → determine results → identify wins/failures → repeat. Kill analysis paralysis; decide and own the results. If a win is unexplained, run with it (transparently) while you dig for the cause.
  • You can’t not let it hurt: sometimes campaigns die for reasons beyond you. Take it personally — clients bet real money on you, and the field has no room for tourists.

Principle 4 Use A Living Plan

Principle 4 — Use a Living Plan

Plan, review, document, repeat. Plans fail when they’re made once and filed; agile ≠ “no planning”. A living plan is organic, reviewed at built-in intervals (guards against both stubbornness and thrash), and sits at the center of every initiative. Kasim’s template lives in Google Sheets (kasim.me/living-plan); components borrowed heavily from DigitalMarketer (CVO, Customer Avatar Worksheet).

Components

Campaign abstract - Marketing mission statement — plain-English narrative; the barometer for every strategic change (“where in the plan does this live?”). - Scope of work — the CliffsNotes of the contract; guards against client scope creep and your own team’s unpaid additions. - S.M.A.R.T. goals — no more than three; quantifiable or they’re wishful thinking (“$100K additional MRR by fiscal year end”, not “more money”). - Key performance indicators — decided with the client; define exactly how each is measured (what qualifies a lead, CPA equation, referral LTV counts). Few data points, wildly important. “That which is measured is managed.”

Client research — company story (soul) · SWOT (treat threats as “perceived threats”; they reveal fears and quick wins) · product/market fit chart · statement of value ([Product/Service] enables [Avatar] to experience [Result] — shockingly hard for clients to fill) · product/service explanation · competitive analysis including alternatives (Southwest↔Greyhound, plastic surgeon↔gym — alternatives are easier to beat and enable silo marketing) · industry analysis (jargon + content hubs for guest posting/link building).

Avatars — the living Avatar definitions.

Regular management - Rocks — big projects against timelines (term from Gino Wickman’s Traction). Every task must map to a rock, or kill the task or add a rock. - Milestones — wins gating bigger moves (100 email users before paid traffic; a CPA threshold before scaling spend). Ask the client: “what would it take to double the campaign?” - Tasks — the living plan holds billable tasks for scope reconciliation; actionable task management lives in the PM tool. - Reports — delivered inside the plan, consistent intervals, same data points every cycle. Report the truth.

Using it

  • Functional: the query point for every major decision — refer, update, redefine. If the plan dies, accountability and direction die with it.
  • Client-facing: reports inside it, so clients live in it. It filters shiny-object syndrome — most dangerous when a campaign starts succeeding and dreams outgrow the plan. Report delivery is when clients ask the most questions; the plan defends your scope.
  • Zero-sum is allowed: paid for three things, asked for a fourth → revision conversation. (Hourly billing inside an agency model caps you — avoid it.)
  • Internally: course-correct within the plan; changes in assumptions are progress markers, not embarrassments.
  • Narrative: the plan becomes a ready-made case study (redact and pretty it up) — and reviewing wins to find the tipping point improves future plans (discovery: split-testing ad copy early was the recurring PPC tipping point).
  • Tooling criteria: cloud-based, globally visible, change-managed, gated, easily referenced/linkable — Google Sheets + Zapier for automations. Build core templates, clone and improve; vertical-specific child templates.

Principle 5 Use Appropriate Tools Effectively

Principle 5 — Use Appropriate Tools Effectively

“A poor workman blames his tools” — but the workman owns the tool choices, so any blame lands on the choice. The classic failure: installing analytics and never looking at it; paying for Infusionsoft features 7 of 10 accounts never touch.

Adoption process

  1. Integration requirements first — list everything the perfect tool must talk to before shopping (ask the WordPress community before picking a form builder).
  2. Core feature set — must-haves vs nice-to-haves in a comparison spreadsheet; reconcile against your model, not shiny features.
  3. Demo and poke holes — annoying but accelerates; reveals company culture and support quality.
  4. Test in your exact use case — the form builder that “integrated with the CRM” but couldn’t pass hidden fields (fatal for PPC tracking).
  5. Purchase — many “set rates” are negotiable; promo codes; cancel after the trial to trigger retention discounts.
  6. Training & accreditation — no time to train = wrong time to adopt. Delegate to a resident expert, then pass down.
  7. Roll out on ONE low-risk campaign → build the SOP → quarterly reviews of the global tool menu. Indecision is the worst decision.

Diagnose before you prescribe

“To a man with a hammer, everything looks like a nail.” Goals, KPIs, milestones before toolsets — or you build solutions for problems you wish clients had. No two clients are alike; no two solutions should be.

Committing to a single solution

Power-user status brings referrals from the vendor, early access, influence over the roadmap, and buying power (Salesforce-consultant entry point; the Facebook-pixel lead-gen agency). Dangers: platform policy shifts (Google’s review-threshold change sized clients out of Shopper Approved), overnight tool death (Optify shut down same-day while taking orders — years of data lost), and lock-in (an Infusionsoft agency can’t serve a HubSpot client). Mitigation: invest in the company as much as the tool — ask how long in business, customer/employee counts, financial assurances, profitability, fundraising plans, contingencies, biggest threats. Better posture: market benefits, recommend tools — sell the outcome, recommend one tool plus two alternatives, let the client decide (plausible deniability). Walk away from clients set on inadequate tools. Price the service-level difference of unsupported tools.

Data and reporting

You can’t report on what you don’t track. Three data sets: (1) report on now — reverse-engineer the first month’s report to find the inputs; (2) may report later — e.g. track key phrases before ever doing SEO (historic baselines + seasonality are gold); (3) actionable only — content performance, device usage, user movement. Missing data usually lives with the client (lead outcomes → introduce a CRM).

Report negative data. Aggregate dashboards that surface only wins are “creatively masking failure” — unethical and blinding. Consistent KPIs = honest campaign health; every unmasked negative is a roadmap item. If you’re afraid of what the data unmasks, you’re not the resource for that practice — bring in someone who is (your value amplifies, not nullifies).

Correlation isn’t causation

“All five failed landing pages were red, so users hate red” builds a house of cards. Check the full data picture: the “lowest-engagement” page was secretly the top call-conversion page once call tracking went in.

Invest in failure

“I’ve just found 10,000 ways that won’t work.” Failure only pays if it informs the next move; receding to the prior state = complete waste.

Pixeling

Can’t retroactively pixel — install pixels on every worthwhile network immediately, even before you advertise there (AdWords traffic today, viable Facebook remarketing audience tomorrow; Ryan Deiss’s future KPI: cost per pixeled user).

Social integration wins

Joomla (technically better) lost to WordPress (easier; ~70% vs 11% of open-source CMS sites) — where the users go, plugins, support, and integrations follow. Social integration trumps most anything else; a shrinking user base is a jump-ship signal.

SaaS best practices + posture

Avoid contracts in a speed-of-light industry · understand pricing models and scaling (per-seat traps) · caution with white-labeling (you become tech support) · verify live support exists · research past the comparison sites (page 3–4 of Google; Glassdoor for behind-the-scenes). Then: become a power user, an advocate, and a referral partner — vendors share your exact client list. And publicize your unique tool use-cases: individual tools are great lead sources.

Principle 6 Use Human Capital Effectively

Principle 6 — Use Human Capital Effectively

No one is a one-person digital marketing machine — not individuals, not single-resource agencies (“no difference between that silo paradigm and a guy in his Grandma’s basement”). Digital mechanisms commoditize instantly; your people are the only true differentiator. Make “seeker of talent” one of your personal KPIs.

Talent is everywhere

Invest in freelancer relationships (pay well, pay on time, forgive small errors): Dmitry, the Eastern European video editor charging US rates for six years — worth every cent, never needs managing. Talent shows up anywhere: the California Pizza Kitchen waitress who became the best business-development hire ever (and later outgrew them — embrace that risk; better to have had them). When a vendor’s PM shines, request them by name; when they hit capacity, ask who they recommend.

Hub and spoke

  • PM = hub: client advocate, internal SME, champion of the strategy, single point of contact shielding the client from specialist noise. Someone must intimately understand the client and own the campaign, or campaigns waver and disintegrate.
  • Specialists = spokes: interdependent tasks need coordination (processes + a PM per campaign). Less “efficient” than other models, but it’s what keeps quality from being a chain that snaps at its weakest link.
  • Autonomy within centralization: a VA (or two) per PM — high-value people spend 30%+ of their day on $10/hour tasks. Let sequential tasks flow without the PM as bottleneck; PM stays informed to tedium on strategy while skipping the minutiae.

Honest expertise

“We do that” is the death rattle. The jack-of-all-trades marketer is a punchline; SEO, PPC, social, email, copywriting, design each demand a specialist. Don’t offer services you can’t staff excellently. You’re the strategist — your job is to know the button needs pressing and find the best button-presser. Utilizing outside help is how you serve the client, not a disservice.

The case for outsourcing

Solutions 8’s AdWords team: top 3% of certified agencies worldwide, Google Premier Partner — full-funnel strategy amplified their value beyond what clients got going direct. The Inc. 500 SEO backend produced results with systems that would’ve taken years to build. Experts dedicated to one vertical stay ahead of daily industry change so you don’t have to. Margins dip; scalability and campaign success compensate. You’re not “cut out” — button pushers need strategists as much as strategists need them.

Invest, don’t expense

Choosing the cheapest vendor for cornerstone work is the expense-vs-investment mistake. Content at $0.02/word from content farms: STOP — DOING — THAT. Landing pages are the conversion bottleneck — Fiverr them and enjoy disappointment. Kasim’s agency is typically unprofitable the first three months of a campaign, building the foundation for retention and ascension. Corollary: if your fee can’t fund an expert, you’re undercharging (or over-offering). Protect the book of vendors: no-hire clauses in client engagements, non-solicitation in vendor agreements.

Delegate

  • Tedious routine tasks → VA (inspect what you expect); keep strategy and reporting on your/the PM’s plate.
  • Track your hours for a few weeks: a $150/hour you doing $15/hour tasks loses $135 every hour. Inventory everything someone else could do, prioritize by time-eaten, go shopping (Fiverr is a gold mine for discovering what you could outsource).
  • Ask per email: “If I weren’t here, who would be handling this?” · Where are the fires? (recurring problems = a resource to delegate — the Facebook-pixel installer who fixed in minutes what took hours) · Grade yourself per service and outsource the Cs.

Related: principle-5-use-appropriate-tools-effectively · next: principle-7-scale

Media & Learning

Principle 7 Scale

Principle 7 — Scale

A campaign becomes truly profitable when it can scale. Scale = synergy + integration + automation. Most teams leave enormous value on the table in redundant, unamplified work — especially with multiple vendors driving one campaign.

Cross-pollinate the learning

Split-test learnings belong to everyone: the winning email subject line informs the social and content teams. Keep an “Avatar learnings” section in the living plan; share notable failures too (mistakes repeat when not shared). With outside resources, push cross-pollination onto the client as their job (you empower, they drive) — or use the friction to make the case for owning the whole campaign.

Content repurposing

The cheapest amplification there is (most content cost is research/prep — yield more than one asset from it). Rules: only repurpose launched content; never let repurposing dictate what you create; start from what the campaign needs. Sequence: content-rich blog → infographic → slides → video (music + voiceover) → Pinterest/SlideShare/YouTube/Vimeo → guest-post material. Precious-metals client: two-to-three weekly market videos became blogs, lead magnets, white papers. Use free round-one repurposing to show new clients the paradigm (a deposit before the ask).

Synergy (1 + 1 = 3)

Continuity ≠ synergy. Continuity: all channels pushing the same message (already hard). Synergy: channels amplify each other — email CTA → follow the social channel for real-time updates; social CTA → email notifications; conditional remarketing by funnel stage (blog-but-no-services visit → lead magnet ad; purchased → value-optimization ad). Cheap high-yield examples: paid-traffic data informing SEO; top-performing broadcasts stitched into the nurture sequence. Sometimes automation is the enemy of synergy — decide with math, and remember short-term money that burns loyalty is “borrowing from a bankrupt future”.

Processes and documentation

Integration without SOPs is spaghetti code — every future change means unraveling the bowl. Document in-app while you build: TRIGGERS AUTOMATION: Zapier > Mailchimp — SEQUENCE: "PPC Audit — thank you and follow up" — a stranger can lift the hood, troubleshoot, and find the next step. Include unique identifiers (user IDs, accounts) and a password manager. Ethics note: clients paid for the pieces, so they deserve to operate the whole — hand over the documentation they need to run without you. Bonus: documented workflows become blueprints for the next client, and gaps in the map reveal missing processes (lead intake exists, post-purchase nurture exists → build the segmentation bridge between them).

Technical integration

Manual processes dilute value and cap growth. The blog example: publishing can auto-notify subscribers, auto-post to social, auto-schedule — what used to eat an hour of someone’s day. Check Zapier / itDuzzit / IFTTT / Centre for connectors; re-check legacy tools for newly added integrations; marketing automation platforms (Infusionsoft, HubSpot, Pardot, Eloqua, SharpSpring, Marketo) as the campaign foundation.

Needle movers vs rock movers

  • Rock mover: necessary but mundane (VA/intern territory).
  • Needle mover: drives long-term, potentially exponential results — where your time belongs. Automate or streamline rock movers (when automation isn’t possible, build tickler systems — submission checklists that trigger the next human step). Irony: building the automation is a needle-mover task.

Automation

  • Test first, automate second — automation without proof of concept is a waste; existing SOPs are pre-validated candidates.
  • Manual steps must live inside automated flows, never as dead ends (automated nurture → task for a salesperson → automation resumes on their update). Dual-pronged: automation triggers and guides manual processes, and manual processes reset the pace of automation.
  • Start with easy wins to build the habit: meeting reminders → itinerary + resource links → attendance confirmation → post-meeting survey. Simple automations are stronger than complex ones.

Media & Learning

Step 1 Clarify Your Core Principles

Step 1 — Clarify Your Core Principles

To use the framework you must believe: - Every person is a miracle with boundless capabilities waiting to be unlocked (not a commodity — job boards read like classified ads for machinery). - The goal is finding people smarter and more capable than you, even where you excel. “Manageable” people need to be managed; peak performers don’t. - Location doesn’t matter (logistical exceptions aside). COVID proved most work is remote-able. Small US businesses can’t compete with big-company benefits or self-employment — overseas, you’re the dream opportunity. Talent in emerging nations is as skilled or more; most businesses only go international for grunt work and get horrible results. Paying multiples of local salary isn’t exploitation — it’s access. - Education and experience are secondary to tenacity and will. “Hire for will, train for skill.” No degree fully qualifies anyone. Requiring “battle-ready” hires means inheriting other employers’ bad habits. The best Client Manager Kasim ever had came from banking knowing nothing about Google Ads — she knew how to handle demanding clients. - The employer-employee relationship should be a big win-win. See success-pillars. - AI doesn’t replace people — it amplifies the right ones. Bill Gates: “Automation applied to an inefficient operation will magnify the inefficiency.” AI creates leverage → businesses get more done with fewer people → those fewer people must be true Pareto Talent.

Related: pareto-talent-framework · the-hire-book

Media & Learning

Step 2 Create A Job Posting

Step 2 — Create a Job Posting

The posting is a marketing piece — a filter and a magnet, written with the marketing hat (never the HR hat). It should sell the vision, set expectations, and include “flytraps”: built-in tests that reveal who actually reads, follows instructions, and shares your values.

Title

Formula: “WANTED! The World’s [Adjective] Remote [Position]” — e.g. “WANTED! The World’s Most Patient Remote Client Manager”. Why it works: grabs attention (all caps + exclamation), title case raises CTR, “world’s most…” sets the bar and filters, “remote” self-selects, and the role is crystal clear (After Effects Editor > Video Editor > Editor). Don’t hire utility players — except Executive Assistants, whose job is the ambiguity.

The heading (flytrap inception)

First line under the title, every posting: “When you apply, please make sure the subject line is: ‘I actually read the instructions.’“ Wrong subject line = auto-archived, never opened.

Anatomy of the posting

  1. Title — see above
  2. Heading — the instructions flytrap
  3. Who we are — personality-forward, attracts and repels; name the HQ (US-based is a draw internationally) and link the website (subtle homework challenge)
  4. What we’re looking for — plain-language overview before the formal description; flattering, reinforcing language (“lifeblood of our organization”)
  5. Job description — ~5 key responsibilities derived from the desired end results (what do they stamp their name on?); qualifications, skills & experience stay deliberately broad — motivated people learn tools on the job
  6. Salary & growth — exact number, never a range (“[Title] starts at $XXX per [interval]” — “starts at” signals ascension); pay ≥10% above the high-water mark; spell out the promotion ladder and that you promote from within
  7. Personality profile — Predictive Index (PI) preferred; describe the traits of people who succeeded in the role; another attract-and-repel moment
  8. “Make sure you’re comfortable with…” (skunks) — always: remote requirements (quiet space, reliable power/internet) and the 60-day trial period; role-specific ones (angry customers, nights/weekends, sales quotas, tight deadlines, legacy mess, repetitive support work)
  9. Our values — your own, in full. Kasim’s: Truth, Responsibility, Heart (originally “love”; softening it is his one regret — real values should be able to scare the wrong people away)
  10. To apply — the center of the flytrap (below)
  11. Close — positive, promise the upside, invite questions (“please don’t hesitate to reach out”), calibrate based on the applications coming in

Application instructions (flytrap center)

  • Resume as a link (not attachment), as a PDF (not .docx/.pages), named Lastname.Firstname.ROLE-NAME.pdf
  • Experience + why you’d be a good fit (one-sentence answers = minimum-effort person)
  • Completed personality quiz link (PI)
  • CEFR language test (efset.org) only when client-facing — C1+ for talking to clients; don’t scare off great candidates with irrelevant grammar requirements
  • “If you were an animal, what animal would you be and why?” — Trojan horse for rigid ideologues (“people aren’t animals” = filtered); great candidates give creative answers
  • “What does this quote mean to you personally? ‘Work is love made visible.’ – Khalil Gibran” — philosophy-of-work probe; use your own meaningful quote
  • Submissions go to name+role@gmail.com — never an HR portal. Email reveals avatar/signature professionalism, custom domains (side hustles), formatting skills. Gmail “+” hack: Kasim+LIEditor@mycompany.com per job board → tracks which board performs.

Auto-reject rules

Didn’t follow instructions · sloppy formatting · negative or sarcastic answers. Archive, never delete (resubmissions happen — track them).

Step 3 Plan Your Distribution Strategy

Step 3 — Plan Your Distribution Strategy

Decide the hiring pool before posting. Five factors (details per region in hiring-regions):

  • Language — accents matter for client-facing roles. Asian accents can trigger negative call-center associations with some US demographics; mild LATAM accents travel well in the US. Flip the logic for UK clients. Think through the customer experience first.
  • Infrastructure — know the real-world frictions: India (healthcare access), Pakistan (power/internet cuts), Colombia (heat costs), Argentina (currency swings), Ukraine (war). Manage people based on their circumstances, with empathy.
  • Workforce specialization — Argentina: economists. India: software devs + the deepest Google Ads pool (Kasim poached Google’s India Ads specialists hitting a glass ceiling). Philippines: graphic design, video editing. Ukraine: cybersecurity, blockchain. Vietnam: mobile apps, animation. But keep the net wide — two of his best employees ever came from Turkey.
  • Time zones — LATAM aligns with US hours (Ivan and Pareto bet on this). South Asia tolerates graveyard shifts; SE Asia and Eastern Europe less so. A few hours of overlap is enough for most roles: deep work + bookend meetings. Avoid asking people to work against their local culture.
  • Culture — be the bridge: be open to their norms, be hyper-communicative about expectations. Most friction irons out within 90 days.

Where to post

  • Stay geographically broad until you find a deep well (the exception: LinkedIn, which has strong pockets everywhere, especially LATAM).
  • Big generic job boards: mostly noise. Marketplaces (Upwork, Fiverr): avoid for hires — the best people there want clients, not jobs.
  • Post to niche boards for the role (designers, devs, closers, financial experts…) and to boards not traditionally remote — some of the best hires didn’t know remote was an option.
  • Communities count as job boards: Facebook/LinkedIn groups, Slack, Discord, WhatsApp, Telegram. Ask moderators first; spamming backfires.
  • Unique “+” email per board to track which sources produce.

If the funnel doesn’t fill, it’s one of two things: the offer isn’t compelling (fix pay/benefits) or traffic is too low (post wider, pay for promoted posts).

Step 4 Filter The Stack

Step 4 — Filter the Stack

Done right, you’re swarmed with applications. Two intentional filtering rounds:

Round 1 — binary filtering

Black and white: did they follow 100% of the instructions or not? - Subject line doesn’t read “I actually read the instructions” → auto-archive, never opened (delegate even this to the EA). - Missing any single flytrap (attachment instead of link, skipped personality test, unanswered question) → archive. - Automate with Gmail filters / Zapier / a trained GPT — refine the process first, then automate. - Archive, never delete — applicants resubmit; you want the history. - Mindset: this is their first date, best behavior. If they can’t follow simple instructions now, they won’t later.

Round 2 — qualitative filtering

Requires judgment (you, a department head, or a well-trained GPT). Archive if: - The submission feels lazy or uninspired. - Answers don’t align with the role or your core values. - Formatting is messy or hard to follow. - Strong sense it’s just not a fit.

Watch your assumptions: unconventional paths may be fast learners, not job-hoppers; no formal experience may mean self-built projects (initiative beats clock-punching). Tenacity and drive > credentials.

Target: 5–10 viable applicants per hire. Keeping more in the mix costs money (paid trials, see step-5-run-the-tryouts).

Step 5 Run The Tryouts

Step 5 — Run the Tryouts

Kasim’s biggest hiring upgrade: skip first interviews entirely. Interviewing is a skill unrelated to the job (the hunting-dog story: the “disobedient” dogs had the best noses — interviews select for interview skill). Offer a paid trial project to everyone on the shortlist right after filtering. This changed who he said yes to.

The trial offer email

Template in the book; beats: - Optional apology for the late reply (“the process was intense”) — if still swamped, just wait to see who follows up (tenacity flytrap, esp. for sales/CM roles). - Specific praise from their submission (personal, not template). - “Here’s the next step, if you’re game: I’d like to pay you $[XX] for what should be under two hours of work.” - Honest framing: interviews rarely tell him anything; the project stays private, never used commercially. - Payment up front via PayPal (or Wise/Payoneer where PayPal is unavailable) — then welcome questions.

Why pay: respect for their time, sets a paid standard, proves you’re not a scam. Rate fairly for the region ($10–20/h covers most). Worst case ~$400 for ten trials vs the cost of a bad hire (“or stick with the traditional model: hire first, then play ‘let’s find out if you suck at your job’“).

The payment flytrap

Send the money, then wait. Discovered by accident: he paid, forgot to send instructions, and one candidate never followed up — just kept the $20. “Thank God I didn’t hire them.” Now standard: money first, who chases the work tells you everything.

Designing the trial

Condense the real weekly task list of someone already doing the job into ~2 hours: - Graphic designer → conceptualize a project from a simple brief - Content creator → explain a complex topic to a total novice - Media buyer → campaign plan integrating multiple ad networks - Client manager → record a Loom video as if they were the CM (stripped references force follow-up questions); the real test is how they deliver bad news — honest, unsugarcoated, solution-championing

Built-in flytraps

  • Wrong login credentials for a required download step → reveals when they start, whether they verify what they need, and how they handle a bump.
  • No deadline → ask them to estimate; procrastinators surface themselves (Monday project, Friday delivery, Thursday panic about credentials = red flag).
  • Back-and-forth during the trial with their would-be department head → easy to work with? clarifying questions? responsive? applies feedback?
  • Final overview video explaining what they did → thought process; can’t explain own work = red flag; refuses camera = dealbreaker for client-facing roles.

Narrowing

Reviewing trials is the most arduous step — delegate it (dept head, someone in the role, or a competent EA). Take notes and share them with every candidate, including rejections (professional courtesy + reputation protection; rejection letter template at TheHireBook.com/Free). Of every 10 completed trials, 3–5 emerge as strong finalists.

Don’t hire straight out of trials — do the interview first (step-6-conduct-the-interviews).

Step 6 Conduct The Interviews

Step 6 — Conduct the Interviews

Interviews are the final filter, not the starting point. By now you’ve seen candidates do real work — the interview confirms what you already suspect. It’s your first live interaction and it sets the tone; treat it more like a sales call than a vetting session (they’re sizing you up too).

The invite

  • Thank them, cite specifics from their project (“we loved it — especially…”), affirm fit (not a job offer).
  • Video, “face to face” — camera-on expected; refusal is a dealbreaker in most cases (cameras build bonds remote work otherwise lacks).
  • For customer-facing roles, a scheduling flytrap: they pick the video tool and send you instructions (“treat me like a client whose technical proficiency you’re unsure of”) — tests clear, non-condescending communication.
  • Sales-role flytrap: cancel the meeting day-of, apologize, ask them to rebook. Grace under cancellation is part of the job; some fail spectacularly.

Rapport

Start every interview by discussing the trial project — specific praise first. Pareto Talent loves talking about their work; it’s the best rapport-builder and gets them to show their true selves.

Kasim’s four questions

  1. “Flash forward five years — the world is perfect, everything went your way. Where are you? What are you doing?” — reveals how to manage, incentivize, and grow them; aspiring entrepreneurs are often the best employees. Non-negotiables to state: at least two years, won’t steal clients or employees, trains their replacement.
  2. “I’m worried you may be overqualified… why is this position right for you?” — surface overqualification early (framework quality attracts PhDs to entry roles); forces them to sell you on starting where the role is; refer back if qualifications get weaponized later.
  3. “Worst-case scenario after the 60-day trial — talk me through it.” — protects people leaving stable jobs; has killed hires who decided the security they had was worth more.
  4. “Are you sure you’re comfortable with [each skunk]?” — walk every skunk from the posting one by one; people rarely complain later about what they explained away themselves.

Personality assessment

Review PI results with the candidate: maps friction with their future manager, and lets you ask hard questions without being the bad guy (“the assessment says…” — you’re just asking about it). Minor red flags (detail gaps, curtness, lateness) surfaced early are manageable; hidden they become real problems.

Close

Always tell candidates where they stand and when they’ll hear back — Pareto Talent is in high demand; silence loses great people. When you know, trust your gut and make the offer.

Step 7 Onboard For Success

Step 7 — Onboard for Success (The First 90 Days)

Hiring is the starting gate, not the finish line. Onboarding should feel like a launch sequence — habits, expectations, and momentum are set here. (Pro-tip: hire multiple people for the same role in a growth phase — team atmosphere in training, no single “new person”, healthy competition.)

Paper people up

International contractor agreements are mostly unenforceable — formalize anyway: legitimacy, clear expectations, professional foundation. Template at TheHireBook.com/Free (PTO, maternity leave, non-disclosure / non-solicitation / non-recruitment / non-compete boilerplate). Make the offer formally: walk the agreement section by section in a meeting, invite questions, encourage them to get it legally reviewed. Transparency builds trust.

Set the pace

  • Assign more work than they can finish (12 units when 10 is realistic) — with the explicit expectation of normal 8-hour days and proactive communication about what does/doesn’t get done.
  • Parkinson’s law: work expands to fill the time allotted. Employees never work harder than in the first 90 days — set the pace early.
  • Easing people in slowly breeds bad habits and a bait-and-switch feeling later. But no busywork: delegate your backlog of important projects — Pareto Talent will blow you away given real shots.

Keep PTO simple and fair

20 paid days off/year, accrued 1.7 days/month, use-it-or-lose-it, same plan for everyone. Contractor agreement states maternity/paternity leave isn’t an offered benefit — but handle committed, returning employees case-by-case and fairly.

Pay on time

Getting paid is a sensitive issue internationally (plenty of “strung along for months” horror stories). Pay on time or early. Processors in order: Payoneer → Wise → PayPal (~90% of the functional globe). Cover the transfer fees — small percentages are significant money in emerging economies.

Stay connected

  • Daily check-ins with new hires (short ones) until confidence is established, then two weekly standing meetings (team + company).
  • Feedback early and often, framed as calibration, paired with positive reinforcement. Tie small stuff to the why (“font usage → we work with brand advocates who obsess over details”). If you can’t connect a strong why, you’re nitpicking.
  • Check-ins should involve the department head or someone directly in the work, or feedback gets diluted.
  • Formally announce when someone passes the 60-day trial — nerve-wracking by design, so make passing it loud and celebratory.

Build team spirit

Remote camaraderie must be intentional: 1. All-hands meeting — weekly town hall: 5-minute engagement game, company health check (goals/KPIs), news, department updates, Q&A, and Open Mic (one employee, up to 10 minutes, any topic — passions, talents, hometowns). 2. Open Mic (above) — surfaces talent and personality you’d otherwise never see. 3. Team connections — standing calls for pods/projects; fun Slack channels (pets, books, shows, music, travel). Shared interests measurably improve collaboration.

Be the incubator

  • Never underestimate them — the EA became Director of Automations, Director of Social Media, CTO and business partner (ivan-bunin). Look within before hiring high-level roles outside.
  • You can’t retain top talent — support their journey instead (prevents “midnight move-outs”, earns referrals, builds the incubator reputation). Includes supporting side hustles (see success-pillars and danish-ashrafi-and-collin-schmelebeck).

Success Pillars

The 5 Success Pillars

“Winners want to win. If you want to hire winners, give them an opportunity that looks and feels like a win.” Core motivators for most employees — vary by company, role, individual:

1. Compensation — pay more because it pays off

  • “There’s nothing more expensive than a cheap employee.”
  • Pay at least 10% above the high-water mark; ideally as much as possible. 2–5x industry average buys 10x–100x output.
  • Paying more takes money stress off the table — sometimes that alone turns mediocre talent into Pareto Talent.
  • Kasim started PH executive assistants at $1,500/month when peers paid $400; by the Solutions 8 exit, multiple PH employees earned US-comparable salaries. That’s how an agency runs 40% margins in a 15% industry.

2. Community

  • Connection is a stronger retention driver than compensation — people stay for the community after outgrowing the pay.
  • Solutions 8: themed Slack channels (music, books, pets, kids, travel), Friday all-hands, and Open Mic — one employee presents 5–10 minutes on anything (guitar solos, succulents, hometown deep dives).
  • Shared values: goals define where you’re going, values define how. The “super-secret trick”: tell people what the values are, frequently.

3. Purpose — make the work meaningful

  • The call-rating team story: monotonous job (listening to and scoring every recorded call — one of only two agencies doing it), reframed as “willing to do what didn’t scale”. Kasim praised them on sales calls, podcasts, stage; celebrated their catches weekly. They stayed years; the team lead Harsh became a shining star.
  • Work doesn’t need to be exciting to be meaningful — people need to see the value they bring.

4. Freedom — flexibility matters more than money

  • 77% of employees say flexible work matters more than a pay raise (People Management poll, 2,000+ respondents; corroborated by HBR and Grant Thornton).
  • “Be as flexible as the role allows.” Output-driven roles: manage on results, not hours. Rules for phone-answering roles still apply.
  • Structure incentives like a game: Solutions 8 ad managers were paid per client managed, uncapped, as long as quality/retention stayed high — clear rules, real rewards, win-win.
  • Trust: no intrusive monitoring software or screenshot demands. “Trust is fragile. It needs to flow both ways. And it should start with the employer.” (Pareto’s no-screen-tracking policy comes straight from this.)

5. Growth — the best talent won’t stay stagnant

  • Pareto Talent is future-minded; show them a path. Spotlight menial-to-promotion stories in postings, interviews, website.
  • The uncomfortable truth: you can’t retain Pareto Talent — you don’t. Retention implies employer entitlement. Keep them as long as you give them a path forward.
  • Help them grow even if it means losing them. Support side hustles — two rules: (1) it can’t directly compete with the full-time job; (2) when they leave, they help find and train their replacement. Side-hustle employees are better: they empathize with the employer, more industrious, more autonomous. And they come back as referral/strategic partners — see case studies.

The 7 Critical Principles of Effective Digital Marketing

The 7 Critical Principles of Effective Digital Marketing — Kasim Aslam (2017)

Published by Stone Soup Hustler Publications, Scottsdale AZ. ISBN 978-1542991001. Format openly borrowed from Covey’s 7 Habits; the core claim is the same diagnosis: the industry runs on a personality ethic (tips, hacks, quick wins — the HubSpot “put ‘video’ in the subject line” example) when lasting success needs a character ethic (principles). Tactics are icing; principles are the cake.

Source: 7 Critical Principles (PDF)

Foundation definitions

  • Digital marketing = relationship building = Content + Context. It is not selling (sales is a byproduct of relationships), not branding (branding designs the house; relationship building invites people to dinner), not advertising (advertising pushes and interrupts; digital marketing pulls and aligns agendas).
  • Push is dead, pull won. Consumers control engagement; attention is now bought by the second at a commoditized premium.
  • Principles are stated as verbs — actions, not concepts.

The principles

Paradigm principles (the WHY — independent, foundational): 1. Empathize — know the person (Avatar), place, and moment 2. Be the first (and last) to give value — deposits before withdrawals, lockstep value 3. Learn, apply & innovate — education as a lifestyle, systematized

Process principles (the HOW — built on the paradigm principles): 4. Use a living plan — a functional, client-visible plan, not a drawer document 5. Use appropriate tools effectively — deliberate adoption, diagnose before prescribing 6. Use human capital effectively — hub and spoke, specialists, delegate 7. Scale — synergy + integration + automation (1+1=3)

Principles 4, 5, 6 interconnect through 7. Missing “life principles” (honesty, diligence) are assumed, not absent.

HIRE — How to Attract, Hire, and Manage the Best Remote Talent in the World

HIRE — Kasim Aslam & Ivan Bunin (2025)

The full hiring operating system of pareto-talent. Free templates referenced throughout: TheHireBook.com/Free (job posting, trial project offer + details, rejection letter, schedule email, contractor agreement, global job board, one-page cheat sheet, workbook). Reviews: TheHireBook.com/Review. Success stories: share on social + tag @KasimAslam → free 5-day training for the new hire.

Book funnel: thehirebook.com — $9.99 hardcover offer, bulk packs (the 10-pack doubles as a $1,000 placement credit), a “We’ll fund your EA for a year” giveaway, and Kasim’s 3XFreedom Skool community.

Source: HIRE (PDF)

Core idea: what is “Pareto Talent”

Elite contributors who consistently deliver 10x, 20x, even 100x the results of their peers. - The Pareto Principle is fractal: of 1,000 people, 200 produce 80% of output; within them, 40 produce 80% of that (64% total); then 8 → 51.2%; then 1.6 → ~41%. One person is effectively responsible for ~25% of an organization’s total output (the gym analogy: 8 superstars out of 1,000 out-produce the other 992; “the one” — Neo — pulls 25%). - Most companies fight this (“key man risk”, quotas, treating people as interchangeable commodities) instead of harnessing it. The play is building your pyramid’s base with the talent others have at the top — massive leverage. - Kasim’s proof: John Moran was ~40% of Solutions 8 revenue; selling = losing that revenue, not spreading clients across “equally viable commodities”. - Only exception found in 20 years: outbound sales (great outbound salespeople don’t look for jobs). - AI angle: AI magnifies whoever operates it — bad people = bad output magnified, extraordinary people = extraordinary output magnified. AI creates leverage, so you only want to scale the exceptional → “a needle in a stack of needles”.

The system

  • pareto-talent-framework — the 7 steps (order is intentional: filter before you interview)
  • success-pillars — compensation, community, purpose, freedom, growth
  • hiring-regions — SE Asia, South Asia, LATAM, Eastern Europe, North Africa & Middle East, Canada

Six beliefs you must hold to use the framework

People are miracles, not commodities · hire people smarter than you · location doesn’t matter · tenacity and will beat credentials · employer-employee should be a win-win · AI amplifies the right people. Details in step-1-clarify-your-core-principles.

Book structure

Introduction (Pareto Talent) → Step 1 Clarify Your Core Principles → Step 2 Create a Job Posting → Step 3 Plan Your Distribution Strategy → Step 4 Filter the Stack → Step 5 Run the Tryouts → Step 6 Conduct the Interviews → Step 7 Onboard for Success (First 90 Days) → Conclusion → Bonus: Hiring Regions → Templates and Resources.

Day1 Notes

Bootcamp Day 1 — Organization & Expectations

Full transcript: day1-transcript

Why this bootcamp

  • 7th cohort; ~3,000 graduates over 6 prior bootcamps; 2M+ people in Argentina have seen their ads; heavy referral flow (referrals = NPS proof).
  • Big commitment by design: 10 days × 2 h + daily homework. Day 1 exists to prove it’s worth it — and to scare off anyone who can’t commit. Numbers are shown openly (see pareto-bootcamp).

Ivan’s story (the origin)

  • Freelancing from 16 (design, dropshipping), $400–600/month, constant switching, balancing university.
  • 2018: EA job at Kasim’s 6-person Arizona agency. Asked $1,000, got $1,200 — “first time it didn’t feel like a scam”.
  • EA → technical team lead → CTO as the agency grew to 60 (Solutions 8). Ran the 2022 sale due diligence → co-founded pareto-talent with Kasim.
  • Exposure compounding: stages at GoHighLevel, awards, masterminds, meeting people like Steve Sims.

Proof & clients

  • First client ever: Tim Bratton — founder of Rhapsody (→ Napster → Spotify) and one of the MP3 inventors. Pareto serves high-level founders who want a real right hand, not a disposable VA.
  • Today: 100+ active founders, 250+ EA community, sister company Architects.com.

The model (find → train → place → support)

Screening is manual and strict (7,000+ applications, ~885 approved; ~9% of applicants made the bootcamp; last cohort 118/10,000 accepted end-to-end). Entrepreneurs are vetted too: intake, onboarding, personality tests.

What a placed right hand gets

$1,000/mo starting full-time (higher with relevant experience), USD via Payoneer/Wise · 20-day PTO (1.7 days/mo accrual) · no screen monitoring (trust-based) · up to $100/mo subscriptions · equipment support (MacBooks) · EA of the Month/Year awards · lifetime replacement guarantee (both ways) · 70+ weekly trainings, 35+ Udemy courses · community, gifts, merch · Juan Cruz helps with legal payment setups.

Mechanics

  • Attendance: 80% nominal, but the final project decides; engaged attendance is a tiebreaker for borderline passes.
  • Timeline to placement is variable — can happen before the bootcamp ends or months later; matching quality beats matching speed.
  • Community platform channels: announcements, info & rules, general, homework, resources, questions.

Rules

Be professional · stay on topic · be polite (instant kick for rudeness, even passive-aggressive) · ask smart questions (Google/AI before asking people) · English only (the bootcamp is English practice) · no spam, no side WhatsApp groups.
