521 01:24:40.450 –> 01:24:50.319 Ivan Bunin: That’s, again, that’s, for us, indicator that, hey, this person does not know how to help themselves in the first place. How can we help them, right?

522 01:24:50.710 –> 01:25:00.559 Ivan Bunin: So that’s why, again, we require, again, basic technical reliance, knowing how to operate a browser, computer, how to download stuff from internet, etc.

523 01:25:01.660 –> 01:25:02.430 Ivan Bunin: Awesome.

524 01:25:03.780 –> 01:25:04.650 Ivan Bunin: Now…

525 01:25:04.930 –> 01:25:10.700 Ivan Bunin: Let’s talk a bit more about communication and a bit more about the actual role of executive assistant, right?

526 01:25:11.040 –> 01:25:21.430 Ivan Bunin: Here’s number one problem that a lot of people get when they start working in a professional environment, that is different, that is more proactive, is that

527 01:25:21.810 –> 01:25:22.860 Ivan Bunin: they…

528 01:25:23.100 –> 01:25:34.250 Ivan Bunin: under-communicate. You communicate less than you need to communicate. For example, let’s say I send you a message, like, hey, can you build this funnel, right?

529 01:25:34.480 –> 01:25:43.250 Ivan Bunin: One of the ideas that a lot of people have is to wait up until they go to the deliverable and only then send the reply. Yes, here we go, right?

530 01:25:43.520 –> 01:25:51.460 Ivan Bunin: And again, build a funnel might be bigger. Let’s, again, compress it. Can you please send me, this presentation that you mentioned yesterday?

531 01:25:52.100 –> 01:26:03.629 Ivan Bunin: Instead of you waiting until you have the full deliverable, you need to first confirm that you received the request, like, hey, yeah, sure, let me check. Hey, Les, thank you, like, I will send you in 2 hours, etc.

532 01:26:04.090 –> 01:26:23.669 Ivan Bunin: So, this acceptance of communication, that’s something that will help you a lot. So, over-communicate. That’s what’s expected of you. You will never be draining if you’re communicating properly. Or again, same thing, if the deadline is going to slip, if you know that you won’t make it, like, communicate it proactively, don’t wait.

533 01:26:24.360 –> 01:26:31.870 Ivan Bunin: Or, if you have a short update on, anything, right, go ahead and give it, rather than wait for a perfect time.

534 01:26:32.400 –> 01:26:40.910 Ivan Bunin: Again, you’ll be needing to ask, like, write in English clearly and all the time. And that’s…

535 01:26:41.100 –> 01:26:46.029 Ivan Bunin: Includes all of the, how do you call them?

536 01:26:46.100 –> 01:27:00.559 Ivan Bunin: abbreviations as well. Like, a lot of you will be tempted to write EA, IA, but this is, like, to Americans, like, that doesn’t mean anything. They have no idea what you’re talking about.

537 01:27:00.610 –> 01:27:12.150 Ivan Bunin: That’s why if you’re looking… if you’re speaking in English, use the abbreviations that are English, right? That would allow you to communicate so much more, efficiently with whoever you’re speaking with, right?

538 01:27:13.300 –> 01:27:16.439 Ivan Bunin: Now, let’s talk about the four C’s of communication.

539 01:27:17.330 –> 01:27:20.019 Ivan Bunin: If you can structure a communication in this way.

540 01:27:20.830 –> 01:27:30.119 Ivan Bunin: you will be so much more efficient in it. And you will see that, artificial intelligence already using the forces of communication better than you.

541 01:27:30.290 –> 01:27:33.049 Ivan Bunin: So, number one, your communication needs to be clear.

542 01:27:33.290 –> 01:27:53.239 Ivan Bunin: You need to be writing not that so you can be understood, but you need to be writing so you cannot be misunderstood. Like, if you will just, understand this first sentence in here, that will already solve all of your problems in communication. Write in a way that there is impossible to misunderstand what you are trying to say.

543 01:27:53.370 –> 01:27:58.960 Ivan Bunin: Right? So each time that you’re writing something, think on how this other person will be reading that.

544 01:27:59.050 –> 01:28:16.969 Ivan Bunin: I’m, even until, like, right now, every time before I hit enter on a message, I cross-check if I wrote the name correctly, if I provided the resources that I mentioned that I will provide, if my communication is clear, if I didn’t make any, like, stupid typos that, are just hilarious, right?

545 01:28:17.480 –> 01:28:30.629 Ivan Bunin: Every single time. And this will never change, so you need to assume this habit, like, immediately, as soon as you can. That is what will allow you to, again, be professional in the first place. Next is concise.

546 01:28:30.880 –> 01:28:38.259 Ivan Bunin: And this is something that a lot of people, miss between 1 and 3. Like, I jumped to the third one, right, to concise.

547 01:28:38.740 –> 01:28:47.569 Ivan Bunin: Because the easiest way to be clear in your communication is to provide so much context that you will overwhelm.

548 01:28:48.330 –> 01:28:51.769 Ivan Bunin: You know these people that write full paragraph words of text to you?

549 01:28:52.470 –> 01:29:12.099 Ivan Bunin: you don’t want to be this person. You want to be able to express your thoughts clearly and concisely, so it’s easier to understand, right? That’s why we use a lot of abbreviations, we use a lot of other things. We try to shorten down. We have a lot of things that are known, that we don’t need to spell out, that’s why we use it, right?

550 01:29:12.170 –> 01:29:13.920 Ivan Bunin: Next is complete.

551 01:29:14.710 –> 01:29:17.210 Ivan Bunin: So, your communication should provide

552 01:29:17.600 –> 01:29:30.550 Ivan Bunin: answers. It shouldn’t, like, lead into the dark, right? It should give all of the information that an entrepreneur or somebody else might need in order to actually be able to help you or to answer you.

553 01:29:30.670 –> 01:29:42.909 Ivan Bunin: Right? So, if you’re mentioning an invoice, like, hey, there was an invoice in your account, I didn’t know if you wanted me to do anything about this. This is a very bad example of communication. It’s not clear, it’s not concise, it’s not complete.

554 01:29:43.170 –> 01:29:47.680 Ivan Bunin: Right? Versus saying sounds like, hey, I received this invoice.

555 01:29:47.930 –> 01:29:56.109 Ivan Bunin: I’m attaching it in here. As I checked, it’s from this client that is already paid. I think it’s a duplicate. Should I go ahead and refund him?

556 01:29:57.390 –> 01:30:02.789 Ivan Bunin: That’s a clear, concise communication with the last pills, which is call to action.

557 01:30:02.790 –> 01:30:19.020 Ivan Bunin: You see what I did in just my, like, thing that I said? I asked, like, should I go ahead and refund him? This is call to action. I’m asking you, hey, tell me what to do. Do I do that or not do that? Call to actions can be different, it can be next steps, like, hey, I prepared the website for you,

558 01:30:20.200 –> 01:30:36.539 Ivan Bunin: let me know if we are good to go ahead and start the marketing for this, right? Or start launching the ads, right? So, in the end, I am finishing with the question, because you need to keep conversation going, right? If your conversation is just stuck, like, hey, there is invoice in email.

559 01:30:37.780 –> 01:30:38.800 Ivan Bunin: And what?

560 01:30:39.130 –> 01:30:42.610 Ivan Bunin: There is no call to action, there is no, like, complete information.

561 01:30:42.990 –> 01:30:50.749 Ivan Bunin: So, you need to start treating your conversation, your communication, as job, as you already doing the deliverable.

562 01:30:51.270 –> 01:30:55.960 Ivan Bunin: Because a lot of people think that communication is something around the job.

563 01:30:56.460 –> 01:31:06.730 Ivan Bunin: Right? It’s… it’s completely irrelevant. Communication is the job. You being able to clearly answer and ask is, like, half the job, to be honest. Right?

564 01:31:08.350 –> 01:31:21.409 Ivan Bunin: That leads me to the next thing that is a part of the right-hand job description, in our opinion. And that’s something that we also, again, recommend you to start practicing here, is end-of-the-day report.

565 01:31:22.460 –> 01:31:32.739 Ivan Bunin: So, you being able to share with the entrepreneur what you were able to do today, and linking it to, concrete deliverables, etc. Here is the reason for that.

566 01:31:33.470 –> 01:31:42.100 Ivan Bunin: This is not to track how you spent your time, but this is for me to be able to set the priorities and be able to be on the same page with you.

567 01:31:42.650 –> 01:31:46.090 Ivan Bunin: Ampi here, like, Ampey never tracked a single hour of her life.

568 01:31:46.240 –> 01:32:01.269 Ivan Bunin: Ever, probably. But she’s still doing these end-of-the-day reports every single day, so I can have all of the material, so if I ask Amy for something, I know that I will get it in the end of the day report. I know that I always can just open my Slack, and I will get it from Ampi.

569 01:32:01.490 –> 01:32:19.990 Ivan Bunin: Because she just never forgets things, for some reason. And again, then it all links to individual things. So we see all of these hyperlinks? Instead of Amphi just saying that, hey, I built this, this, and this. No, like, she goes ahead and links it to a particular resource that she delivered that I can click on and get access to immediately.

570 01:32:20.280 –> 01:32:27.540 Ivan Bunin: And then, if I know that I’m looking for something that Ampi done last week, all I need to do is scroll back to this end-of-the-day report, and I will find it.

571 01:32:28.150 –> 01:32:38.959 Ivan Bunin: This is what end of the report does. The other thing it does is it gives your entrepreneur the understanding that you are working. Here’s what I mean by that.

572 01:32:39.080 –> 01:32:45.770 Ivan Bunin: If you remember the point number 5 that I showed you, a lot of entrepreneurs were burned by virtual assistants before.

573 01:32:45.910 –> 01:32:48.000 Ivan Bunin: They worked with somebody who was

574 01:32:48.430 –> 01:32:59.879 Ivan Bunin: not integrus, who was dishonest, and didn’t deliver what they promised. So whenever you are stepping in, in majority of cases, you are stepping in into already a mess.

575 01:33:00.070 –> 01:33:06.090 Ivan Bunin: and some of the limiting beliefs that entrepreneurs might have. End of the day reports fix that.

576 01:33:06.830 –> 01:33:26.239 Ivan Bunin: they show to entrepreneur, hey, you can trust me, here is… like, I can do stuff, here is what I can do, and then they have a feeling that they don’t need to be watching you. They don’t need to record the screen, they not need to ask you to do a selfie in front of the computer every 2 hours, right? Because this is how you build trust, this is how you build integrity.

577 01:33:26.370 –> 01:33:31.870 Ivan Bunin: You do it first. You show that you are trustworthy, and that’s what it means, right?

578 01:33:32.530 –> 01:33:36.240 Ivan Bunin: That’s, again, just one of the examples of this end-of-the-day reports, right?

579 01:33:38.050 –> 01:33:43.050 Ivan Bunin: Okay, next is the productivity, what I mentioned to you, right?

580 01:33:43.650 –> 01:33:48.820 Ivan Bunin: We are… Expecting you to be able to manage yourself.

582 01:33:52.970 –> 01:34:00.859 Ivan Bunin: this will not be a good position for you. And if you… if you was being told what to do right now in your job, you can change.

583 01:34:01.150 –> 01:34:10.770 Ivan Bunin: Right? But you need to make this decision on your end that, hey, I will not be waiting for the last deadline. I will not be waiting for somebody to remind me. I will just…

584 01:34:10.910 –> 01:34:12.509 Ivan Bunin: Go ahead and do that.

585 01:34:13.840 –> 01:34:16.929 Ivan Bunin: My business partner, Kasim has a very…

587 01:34:21.410 –> 01:34:31.230 Ivan Bunin: is that… Trust is, sorry, is that… Forgiveness better than permission.

588 01:34:32.970 –> 01:34:38.809 Ivan Bunin: So, forgiveness… Forgiveness better than permission.

589 01:34:39.740 –> 01:34:42.120 Ivan Bunin: So, what does it mean? Is that…

590 01:34:43.620 –> 01:34:57.730 Ivan Bunin: it’s better for you to say sorry that I went ahead and I was way too proactive, and I built you a new website because I thought you will need that, versus you asking for a permission, hey, can I please, like, try doing this website?

591 01:34:58.060 –> 01:35:02.090 Ivan Bunin: If you will just be proactive and ask for the forgiveness later, it’s better.

592 01:35:04.150 –> 01:35:10.700 Ivan Bunin: So that’s the… something that I would like you to… to assume, to… to start thinking from a perspective of, right?

593 01:35:11.710 –> 01:35:12.470 Ivan Bunin: Oh!

594 01:35:12.810 –> 01:35:15.700 Ivan Bunin: No.

595 01:35:17.010 –> 01:35:25.120 Ivan Bunin: A task is not done until the person who asked knows that it’s done, until it’s clean, right? This is something that we call, close the loop

596 01:35:25.690 –> 01:35:29.579 Ivan Bunin: Each task that you open, or each project, is an open loop.

597 01:35:29.700 –> 01:35:33.619 Ivan Bunin: And you are the person to close this loop and take it home.

598 01:35:33.760 –> 01:35:47.919 Ivan Bunin: to actually finish it, to push it through the finish line, right? That falls on your end. The easiest way to think about that, the easiest way to implement that, each time that there is an email or a message, your message should be the last one.

599 01:35:49.450 –> 01:35:52.169 Ivan Bunin: Even if it’s like, okay, I got it, thank you so much.

600 01:35:53.070 –> 01:35:59.250 Ivan Bunin: Your message is the last one. That way, you will ensure that you never leave unfinished things.

601 01:35:59.830 –> 01:36:12.059 Ivan Bunin: Because the worst thing you can do is not finish something and not do it, right? Because you just, hey, I just forgot. Hey, it just slips through my mind, right? Another quote that Kasim told me on my very first interview with him.

603 01:36:17.850 –> 01:36:20.249 Ivan Bunin: And you do 9 of them perfectly.

604 01:36:20.800 –> 01:36:25.080 Ivan Bunin: But you forget about one of them, You are useless to me.

605 01:36:26.580 –> 01:36:40.130 Ivan Bunin: It sounds very rude, it sounds very bad, like, I did 90%. In university, 90% is great. 90% is what gets you the application, right? But in a perfect world, the idea is, is that if you missed one of 10,

606 01:36:40.740 –> 01:36:43.070 Ivan Bunin: Then chances are you missed more.

607 01:36:43.470 –> 01:36:46.010 Ivan Bunin: Because this is just the one that I was able to find.

608 01:36:46.340 –> 01:36:50.159 Ivan Bunin: Chances are you… there will be additional sleeps that we will not find.

609 01:36:50.380 –> 01:36:56.859 Ivan Bunin: So, therefore, if you’re taking something in, you need to push it through the finish line, you need to finish it, you need to close this loop.

631 01:39:31.900 –> 01:39:41.679 Ivan Bunin: you have two fields, you have first name, last name. I recommend you, from the very get-go right now, think on what are the names that you would like to be used in your day-to-day, right?

Media & Learning

Day2 Notes

Bootcamp Day 2 — AI & Context Engineering

Full transcript: day2-transcript

The one big idea

Context > prompts. An LLM predicts the next token from training data; with no context it reaches for the generic internet answer (the exercise: ask ChatGPT for a random number 1–25 → almost everyone gets 17). Generic in → generic out; “trash in, trash out”, and AI amplifies it. Your private context is the only thing no one else’s AI has — that’s the edge.

Four kinds of AI (orientation)

Supervised (learns from labeled examples) · unsupervised (finds patterns/groupings) · reinforcement (trial and error) · generative (text, image, agents — the daily-driver kind). Modern agentic tools blend them; generative is the one that runs on context.

Marry one tool

Pick one LLM and go deep — switching tools at every model release keeps you playing instead of compounding. Pareto’s pick: Claude (chat free tier; Claude Code paid unlocks the real workflows). All the “old” automation glue (n8n-style) increasingly lives inside Claude Code.

Context sources (mine these)

  1. Call recordings — Fathom (free) records and transcribes; ~2,000 calls at Pareto. Feed a transcript to Claude → summaries, promised deliverables, blockers, follow-up drafts.
  2. YouTube transcripts — show transcript / copy, paste as grounding truth for tasks (e.g. building Meta campaigns from Nathan/BlueSense’s long-form instead of generic AI advice).
  3. Google Drive — videos auto-transcribed; contracts/docs feed directly.
  4. Websites — scrape (FireCrawl for full-page markdown) so AI knows your actual offer.
  5. Dictation — type less, say more. Claude has native dictation (Cmd+D); Whisperflow dictates anywhere with a global dictionary (names, acronyms) — under ~140 wpm typing, dictate instead. Dictation naturally produces the context typing compresses away.
  6. Email threads — feed whole threads, not single emails.

You are the context source

No docs yet? Have AI interview you (“ask 20 questions, one by one”) — dictate answers, and the resulting one-pager becomes reusable context you never have to repeat. This is exactly how Pareto’s internal SOPs were written.

Markdown is the AI language

LLMs consume text best; PDFs must be converted to text first. The Obsidian second brain is just ~6,000 markdown files of context feeding AI — that’s why it outperforms vanilla AI. Part of the EA job is mining and building this for the entrepreneur (day 3 continues).

Homework culture

Transcribe every bootcamp day, extract best practices, and let AI use them — practicing the exact workflow the job requires. Final project will include the chats with AI as evidence.

Media & Learning

Day6 Notes

Bootcamp Day 6 — Websites, Conversion & Qualifiers

Full transcript: day6-transcript

The hero section is the website

  • ~93% of visitors see the hero; ~50% ever reach the sections below it (Microsoft Clarity scroll data). Compress the whole pitch into one screen: title (pain-point clarity), sub-headline, CTA, attributes, social proof, rich media.
  • Clarity beats creativity — plain pages with image + button consistently outconvert creative ones. Pick clarity first, add creativity later.
  • Contrast trick: squeeze your eyes — whatever still pops is what visitors see. The CTA button should win (avoid backgrounds/text competing with it). No background patterns “for no reason”: if you can’t find one site on Dribbble doing it well, it’s a bad idea.
  • Titles: display-style, condensed spacing (less than body text), few lines.
  • Real imagery/video (even one custom clip) kills the “AI website” feel. Social proof: badges (stars + count), reach out for testimonials, trade a gift for one; alternatively serve counts (people served, followers, notable names).
  • Microsoft Clarity (free): heat maps, scroll maps, click maps, session recordings — watch how people actually use the page (decisions happen in ~1 second).

Conversion

  • Conversion = one state → another, with commercial intent: sale, lead (form submit — delayed gratification), click.
  • Funnels by price: under ~$300 → straight to checkout. Expensive offers need steps: visit → qualify (form) → book call → buy.
  • Thank-you page: the first value delivery — tell them exactly what happens next; it cures buyer’s remorse (“you did the right thing; here’s what’s next; problems? go here”). Best version delivers something immediately (lead magnet).
  • The Kasim workshop example: landing page → qualifier form → conditional logic → qualified: booking calendar / not qualified: thank-you page. Two conversion events to measure.

Qualifier forms

  • Built in GoHighLevel (vibe-coded forms lack the database/automation tie-ins).
  • Questions must be sortable — dropdowns/radio, not free text; budget, company size, expected outcome with buckets.
  • Conditional logic: if X then Y (budget < $1,000 → no-fit page; ≥ $1,000 → calendar). Redirects by answer.
  • Why qualify: calendar time is the scarce resource — cold Instagram traffic is mostly not a fit yet.

Website teardown patterns (from homework review)

Repetition kills (same card layout three times; duplicated value props) — vary section styles to keep hooking. One primary CTA (secondary CTAs and button-shaped pills distract). Don’t overload the hero. Storytelling sites suit art, not conversion — people don’t scroll.

Media & Learning

Day7 Notes

Bootcamp Day 7 — AI Image & Video Generation

Full transcript: day7-transcript

Prompting images well

  • Iterate vs regenerate: close-but-wrong → iterate on the same image with feedback; totally wrong → rewrite the prompt. AI improves as you steer it.
  • Prompt recipe: (1) what the image is for and where it lives (hero section vs ad vs banner dictates output), (2) the style guide (fonts, colors, vibe — save as a reusable preset), (3) palette screenshots / reference images (“this vibe, this face”). Context keeps output from feeling like AI fluff.

Tools

  • ChatGPT images, Ideogram (ideogram.ai — strong for text/logos; browse others’ prompts as a style school), Midjourney (style references/seeds, style blending — best for heavy creative work), OpenArt (cheap; free credits via their Discord), Higgsfield (all-in-one: many image + video models, ~$1,000 in credits produced Pareto’s Nuno hook videos; “if the videos can’t make $1,000 they’re not being used right”).
  • Canva — the workhorse: templates (nail customizing templates and you’re done), brand kit, background remover, DreamLab AI. Photopea (Photoshop online) for advanced masks; WhatFont to identify fonts.
  • Amparo’s workflow: second brain → audience → pain points × angles → generate prompt batches → run 10 parallel chats pasting prompts → bring results into Canva templates → variants. Inspiration: Facebook Ad Library (facebook.com/ads/library — see what competitors pay to run) and Pinterest; have AI deconstruct a winning ad into a reusable master prompt.
  • Real campaign proof: the ad Amparo showed ran ~$10,000 across campaigns for the VibeCode incubator workshops. AI proves concepts cheap; scale winners manually.

AI video

  • HeyGen — AI avatars from photos/videos of a person; dictate script, pick voice, generate.
  • Higgsfield Cinema Studio + ElevenLabs — voice cloning (“scary good”; also powers AI phone calls via High Level) for character-accurate hooks.
  • AI b-roll to illustrate points when you lack footage.
  • Candela’s editing stack: Opus Clip (started as long-form→shorts repurposing, now general editing), OpenArt for cheap generation (still-image first, video only after the frame is right).

Guiding principle

Always generate for the end use — an image nobody pays for is a toy. Creativity on top of commercial intent; AI lets you test wild ideas cheap, then scale the winners.

Day8 Notes

Bootcamp Day 8 — Traffic & Digital Marketing

Full transcript: day8-transcript

The mental model: a busy street

Traffic = real people with real intentions. Storefront equivalents: signage/banners (ads), the flyer guy (outreach, ~1% conversion — cold is hard), the unpaid promoter (organic advocacy). Online works identically.

Taxonomies

  • Organic vs paid: organic isn’t free — it costs time/salary, and it converts slowly (long-term investment). Paid buys placement and platform, nothing more: the offer + creative still decide whether it works.
  • Outbound/inbound × hot/cold: outbound-hot = messaging warm audiences (commenters, subscribers); inbound-cold = intercepting people with buyer signals. Think in this 2×2 for every campaign.

TOFU / MOFU / BOFU

  • People enter the funnel at different awareness stages — optimize each stage, not just the bottom.
  • BOFU (pain + aware + ready): Google Ads (search = existing intent), referrals, warm email to past buyers. MOFU (aware, comparing): Facebook/Instagram/LinkedIn ads, comparison content. TOFU (unaware): generic YouTube, podcasts, social content — educate first.
  • All three matter: a tiny BOFU converting great still yields 3 customers — build MOFU and TOFU above it and the same rates yield 50.
  • Unproven products (Kickstarter-style) can only start at TOFU — nobody searches for what they’ve never heard of.

Everything that can break (the real funnel)

Ad seen → click → page loads → content reads → button works → form submits → automation fires → thank-you page → conversion tracked. Each step leaks. The game is compounding small percentage wins at every stage, with AI handling most of the verification that used to be manual.

Thank-you page & buyer’s remorse

Deliver immediately (TheHireBook free-book flow is the model); reassure, state next steps, objection-handle. Buyer’s remorse is real — the thank-you page is where you fix it.

Personal brand = moat

Products and prices get copied; identity, voice, and values don’t (Coca-Cola invented Santa to sell Coke in winter — and now owns him).

Audience research

  • Mine what you already have: Fathom sales-call transcripts → paste into Claude with the second brain → extract pains, frustrations, why they bought. One call is an anecdote; 100 calls is an ICP.
  • Also: Reddit threads, YouTube comments, review sites — people literally describe their problems in their own words. Ask AI to crawl these specifically (generic “find my ICP” fails).
  • Ask customer support who they love/hate; check LTV (the recurring whitening patient vs the one-cavity teenager).
  • ICP vs TAM: Pareto’s TAM ≈ 3M US businesses; ICP ≈ 1M (owners, ~$500K+ revenue, not solo startups). Smaller TAM = less competition and higher price — a balance, not a virtue.
  • The payoff — customer’s own words reused in marketing: “I’m the bottleneck in my own company. I built a company and now I work in it as a job. I wanted a business that would give me freedom, but instead I work 12 hours a day.”

ICP definition exercise (Pareto example)

Business owners · revenue ~$500K+ · not solo founders · decision-maker · pain: the founder is the bottleneck.

Day9 Notes

Bootcamp Day 9 — EA Core Skills (Inbox, Calendar, Security)

Full transcript: day9-transcript

Inbox

  • “You’re not hired to answer emails — you’re hired to close the loops.” Inbox zero: the inbox is a to-do queue, not a notifications feed. Can’t close a loop yet? Proactive communication: acknowledge + ETA.
  • Gmail is the standard (open API → connects to every AI tool; only ~15–20% of entrepreneurs are elsewhere). Shortwave on top (free plan): to-do grouping with context notes, built-in AI chat (sorts, drafts in your voice, schedules from your calendar, contextual search), multiple inboxes in one place, bulk archive. It’s still Gmail underneath — connect Claude to the Gmail account, not to Shortwave.
  • Cleaning a neglected inbox: set a cutoff date with the entrepreneur (30 days; negotiate 60/90), bulk-archive everything older, then kill the 80/20 of notification senders. Archiving ≠ deleting — everything stays findable. Google Takeout export calms “what if you delete something” fears.
  • The rulebook: document email rules with the entrepreneur (Amazon notification → archive unless failed delivery; client email → draft; pissed client → notify immediately). You write them down because you’ll eventually hand the inbox to someone else.
  • Access stages: 1) they forward single emails, you draft · 2) delegated access — you clear spam and prepare drafts (drafts save ~80% of reply time; spot-on drafts just get sent) · 3) you reply to ~90% yourself, drafting the unsure 10%. Password access is the true right-hand level (unlocks calendar + connected tools) — with a strong, non-personal password.

Security

  • You carry liability when you hold access (the hacked-Facebook-ads story). 2FA or passkeys everywhere.
  • One strong master password for a password manager (Bitwarden, or Apple Keychain); generated unique passwords for everything else. Test strength at Password Monster — AI cracks weak ones in seconds. Trick: a full sentence (spaces allowed) from a favorite song/movie line.

Calendar

  • Calendar management = Tetris with someone’s time, not booking empty slots.
  • Time blocking: physically block deep work so booking tools can’t fill it. Entrepreneurs must work on the business (marketing, sales, strategy) — they’ll resist giving up operator meetings; that pushback is part of the job.
  • Mirror/ghost events: duplicate a meeting on the same slot without the other party, name it clearly, put all prep details in the description — private briefing notes attached to the calendar.
  • Color coding: gray = blocked/personal, colors = meeting types.
  • Buffers: 10 min pre + 10 min post — calls run long; back-to-back sales calls are how deals die mid-pitch. Ask preferences (some founders cap 3 meetings/day).
  • Batching: group similar calls (Ivan: all 1:1s Wednesday, all group calls Friday) — context-switching is exhausting.
  • Time zones: learn the 4 continental US zones; use worldtimebuddy.com; write times US-style (2 PM EST, never 14:00); Pareto HQ = Scottsdale, MST — no daylight saving, so March/November shifts break relative times by an hour — plan ahead. When someone says “2 PM”, assume their time and look up their location instead of asking.
  • Subscribe to all of the entrepreneur’s relevant calendars (personal, other companies) before booking anything.
  • Booking links: Google Calendar’s built-in appointment schedules are free and killed Calendly for basic use.

Rookie mistakes (everyone makes them once)

Wrong time zone booked · back-to-back days · using the calendar as a record instead of a plan · verbal agreement with no invite sent · daylight-saving drift · checking only one calendar.

565 01:13:07.090 –> 01:13:09.700 Ivan Bunin: Then, let’s continue.

566 01:13:16.310 –> 01:13:18.260 Ivan Bunin: Big topic, project management.

567 01:13:18.910 –> 01:13:21.750 Ivan Bunin: A lot of the things that we are doing.

568 01:13:22.070 –> 01:13:25.460 Ivan Bunin: We will need to be able to manage them as bigger projects.

569 01:13:25.780 –> 01:13:26.790 Ivan Bunin: Because…

570 01:13:26.980 –> 01:13:34.339 Ivan Bunin: they consist from a lot of different things. So let’s dive into, again, understanding what it is and how it works. First of all, let’s set up

571 01:13:34.730 –> 01:13:38.230 Ivan Bunin: What is project management? What is project versus what is task?

572 01:13:38.670 –> 01:13:42.029 Ivan Bunin: Right? What is a project? What is a task?

573 01:13:43.400 –> 01:13:45.669 Ivan Bunin: It’s a very interesting question, because

574 01:13:45.770 –> 01:13:50.590 Ivan Bunin: There is no, like, definition, like, you can try to define it, but here is how I look at that.

575 01:13:51.760 –> 01:13:54.490 Ivan Bunin: It depends on time, to be honest.

576 01:13:55.010 –> 01:13:55.930 Ivan Bunin: Time.

577 01:13:56.890 –> 01:14:03.280 Ivan Bunin: If, making… If making dinner takes me 2 weeks.

578 01:14:05.060 –> 01:14:16.560 Ivan Bunin: Then it’s a project, it’s not a task. If making dinner takes me, like, an hour, it’s a task. This is how I look at this, right? So, the difference between tasks and projects is that

579 01:14:17.140 –> 01:14:25.120 Ivan Bunin: Projects will need much more time, resources, and energy in order to get delivered. And here is why it’s so important right now.

580 01:14:25.220 –> 01:14:27.919 Ivan Bunin: Previously, if you would ask me.

581 01:14:29.030 –> 01:14:43.470 Ivan Bunin: Building a landing page, I would say it’s a project, because you need to prepare all of the materials, prepare all the, like, images, you need to design, you need to choose what architecture we are going to use, what is the CMS, etc. Right now, building a landing page is a task.

582 01:14:44.310 –> 01:14:51.330 Ivan Bunin: Like yesterday, again, I asked Gaspar to jump in and build this quick landing page, the Hire book.

583 01:14:51.480 –> 01:14:52.390 Ivan Bunin: Bree.

584 01:14:52.640 –> 01:14:53.870 Ivan Bunin: Free book.

585 01:14:55.190 –> 01:15:02.549 Ivan Bunin: Like, he built this page, like, rebuilt it, he copied that, and then added some other things there. He’d done this, like, in 20 minutes.

586 01:15:02.940 –> 01:15:04.839 Amparo Linares: Can we? Can we see your screen?

587 01:15:05.050 –> 01:15:06.110 Ivan Bunin: Oh, sorry.

588 01:15:06.420 –> 01:15:07.230 Amparo Linares: Hehe.

589 01:15:07.230 –> 01:15:08.930 Ivan Bunin: Yeah, here.

590 01:15:09.500 –> 01:15:17.790 Ivan Bunin: So the whole page again, it was duplicated from what we had and then move forward. Or again, the other like here, Pareto Talent slash workshop.

591 01:15:19.680 –> 01:15:28.499 Ivan Bunin: This page, again, same thing. It took, like, an hour. So, what I’m saying, again, if we are talking about the project, a lot of that depends on

592 01:15:28.670 –> 01:15:30.280 Ivan Bunin: Your capabilities?

593 01:15:30.410 –> 01:15:39.180 Ivan Bunin: And the time that it would take. So if you think again that something deserves to start being project managed.

594 01:15:39.610 –> 01:15:52.949 Ivan Bunin: then again, I highly recommend you to understand why in the first place. Because not everything needs to be complicated. Some things, again, we just need to straighten up. But if we are talking about real projects, so again, real project is launching the Bootcamp, for example.

595 01:15:53.060 –> 01:16:17.190 Ivan Bunin: That’s not a task. It would take quite a while because for launching the Bootcamp, I need to build the agenda, build the deck, build the landing page, build the funnel, build the pipeline, build the automation, build the ads, run the ads, etc. So like there’s a lot of moving pieces. You cannot just execute it like that. That’s why this is a project. This is a bigger thing, right? That’s how I recommend you to think about, again, projects versus tasks.

596 01:16:17.190 –> 01:16:17.980 Ivan Bunin: Right.

597 01:16:18.480 –> 01:16:22.720 Ivan Bunin: All of the projects can be broken down into four stages, right?

598 01:16:23.420 –> 01:16:30.640 Ivan Bunin: Stage number one is the problem. It’s understanding what is that that we are trying to do? What is the thing that we want to achieve?

599 01:16:30.810 –> 01:16:33.300 Ivan Bunin: Or solve with this project.

600 01:16:33.640 –> 01:16:36.750 Ivan Bunin: Because if there is no problem, guess what? There is no project.

601 01:16:37.590 –> 01:16:42.299 Ivan Bunin: Why do we do that in the first place if we are not solving or not doing anything? Right.

602 01:16:42.640 –> 01:16:44.440 Ivan Bunin: It’s just a piece of work, right?

603 01:16:46.870 –> 01:16:59.170 Ivan Bunin: Here again, an example project. What would be our best insurance company for our business? Right. Analyzing all of that, understand that there is actual problem. Like do we even need to change this?

604 01:17:00.070 –> 01:17:11.989 Ivan Bunin: Do we already have a business insurance? Maybe we don’t need to change this. So that’s something that Kasim hated and loved about working with me a lot, because I would question every single problem he has, because majority of the problems, he didn’t have them.

605 01:17:12.160 –> 01:17:27.839 Ivan Bunin: He imagined them, he started thinking about them, went into his head or saw somebody else doing that and decided we need to do the same, etc. But once you start uncovering that, you realize there’s like no need. Right. So again, in our case, problem, I need talented people. That’s a problem.

606 01:17:28.060 –> 01:17:29.939 Ivan Bunin: Right. Next, plan.

607 01:17:31.200 –> 01:17:34.730 Ivan Bunin: Once you understand that there’s a problem, you need to plan the execution.

608 01:17:34.910 –> 01:17:37.820 Ivan Bunin: What is that that we will be doing in this project?

609 01:17:38.620 –> 01:17:43.969 Ivan Bunin: In all of the projects, there’s usually a couple of the aspects. Number one is.

610 01:17:44.570 –> 01:17:45.450 Ivan Bunin: People.

611 01:17:46.080 –> 01:17:50.999 Ivan Bunin: Who will be involved in this project? Who needs to participate in this project together with me?

612 01:17:51.470 –> 01:17:57.310 Ivan Bunin: Number two is time. By when we need this project delivered. What is the deadline for the project?

613 01:17:58.040 –> 01:18:09.469 Ivan Bunin: And number three are the resources. The resources can be money, tools, access, whatever we need in order to dedicate to this project. So for example, Bootcamp project, we showed again ads yesterday, etc.

614 01:18:10.030 –> 01:18:11.130 Ivan Bunin: I need…

615 01:18:11.260 –> 01:18:18.449 Ivan Bunin: Ampy’s help with the agenda. I need Virginia’s help with the community. I need, again, Gaspar’s help with the ads.

616 01:18:19.250 –> 01:18:26.310 Ivan Bunin: I need to do it before, the beginning of October, because we need talent for, again, October.

617 01:18:26.440 –> 01:18:32.689 Ivan Bunin: I need $5,000, I need GoHighLevel, a Cloud subscription, And that’s pretty much it.

618 01:18:33.230 –> 01:18:39.019 Ivan Bunin: So this is how you, again, look into the projects. What is that that you actually need in order to move forward, right?

619 01:18:39.490 –> 01:18:42.659 Ivan Bunin: Plan this before you even start, again, executing anything.

620 01:18:43.530 –> 01:18:45.059 Ivan Bunin: Next is the progress.

621 01:18:45.190 –> 01:18:49.140 Ivan Bunin: This is especially if you are, like, an employee.

622 01:18:49.600 –> 01:19:06.780 Ivan Bunin: you will have stakeholders, like, people interested in the delivery of this project. So, in my case, again, it’s Amparo Gaspar Virginia who need to report on, again, what’s going on, right? So… As you’re building up the project, you want to be tracking if, you are…

623 01:19:07.690 –> 01:19:11.070 Ivan Bunin: Hitting the timeline, if you’re hitting the deadline that you need.

624 01:19:11.290 –> 01:19:21.089 Ivan Bunin: If everything goes according to plan, if you planned that we’ll build landing page and if it’s actually being built right now, right? And if you have enough resources.

625 01:19:21.870 –> 01:19:22.630 Ivan Bunin: Right.

626 01:19:23.200 –> 01:19:29.570 Ivan Bunin: So, you need to be reporting on that to whoever is stakeholder. So, in your case, majority of cases, it will be your entrepreneur.

627 01:19:29.850 –> 01:19:36.079 Ivan Bunin: Because project without the progress tracked, It’s not going anywhere.

628 01:19:36.700 –> 01:19:46.950 Ivan Bunin: Your entrepreneur, like, worst case scenario, they will just think again that you are scamming them and you are not actually doing that. And again, my business partner, Kasim, has this problem sometimes with people.

629 01:19:47.450 –> 01:19:53.960 Ivan Bunin: Where they’re doing amazing thing, biggest project ever, but they never actually said to anyone about that.

630 01:19:54.820 –> 01:19:55.500 Ivan Bunin: Right.

631 01:19:56.850 –> 01:19:58.710 Ivan Bunin: And lastly, present.

632 01:19:59.090 –> 01:20:01.139 Ivan Bunin: So, presentation of the project.

633 01:20:02.720 –> 01:20:06.679 Ivan Bunin: How did you achieve this? Did you show again what has been done?

634 01:20:07.940 –> 01:20:23.540 Ivan Bunin: Did you, again, deliver all of the things, right? So, for example, if you are talking about the Bootcamp, the presentation of that should be a folder that will have all of the ads, all of the copy, all of the ideas, or, like, built-out workflows with the proper links to them, etc.

635 01:20:24.150 –> 01:20:25.949 Ivan Bunin: That’s the delivery, right?

636 01:20:27.420 –> 01:20:28.140 Ivan Bunin: Perfect.

637 01:20:29.070 –> 01:20:29.940 Ivan Bunin: Now.

638 01:20:30.160 –> 01:20:48.200 Ivan Bunin: let’s talk about, work breakdown structure, or basically just hierarchy of things. Because this is something, again, a lot of people get, get wrong whenever they get bigger tasks. I personally just, like, the last couple of months, I had 3 calls with different, right hands on our pool.

639 01:20:48.450 –> 01:20:49.660 Ivan Bunin: who were stuck.

640 01:20:50.470 –> 01:20:51.999 Ivan Bunin: They received a task.

641 01:20:52.550 –> 01:20:58.659 Ivan Bunin: That they think is a task, but it was a project, and they didn’t know even how to approach it, how to start it. What do I need to do?

642 01:20:58.720 –> 01:21:14.160 Ivan Bunin: Because of how big it is. This is what we are talking about, again, VBS, about the work breakdown structure, right? It’s basically very simple. It’s just hierarchical decomposition, right? How do we understand what do we need to do at any given time, right?

643 01:21:14.390 –> 01:21:16.250 Ivan Bunin: Let me show you an example of this.

644 01:21:21.300 –> 01:21:25.349 Ivan Bunin: Do you guys want to give some project examples, or do you want me to come up with some?

645 01:21:31.830 –> 01:21:33.350 Ivan Bunin: 1, 2, 3, stole.

646 01:21:35.390 –> 01:21:41.310 Ivan Bunin: An app, final project, final project. That’s a good idea, final project.

647 01:21:41.520 –> 01:21:44.199 Ivan Bunin: Python project. Let me think about that.

648 01:21:44.700 –> 01:21:50.499 Ivan Bunin: Okay, yeah, given that you are already on day 9, we can do final project. So, let’s say you have project.

649 01:21:52.740 –> 01:21:54.530 Ivan Bunin: That’s called final, right?

650 01:21:56.470 –> 01:21:58.010 Ivan Bunin: This is a code name.

651 01:21:58.930 –> 01:22:10.509 Ivan Bunin: So, if I just tell you again that you need to complete… okay, no, it’s… let’s do something different. Let’s do some… some real project, like, one thing, right? And app… app is a good one, let’s do app.

652 01:22:11.180 –> 01:22:11.980 Ivan Bunin: App.

653 01:22:13.070 –> 01:22:22.109 Ivan Bunin: So your entrepreneur comes to you and tells you that again, we need to build an app. If they just come to you, hey, I need an app that will be social media for founders of some.

654 01:22:23.750 –> 01:22:32.349 Ivan Bunin: That’s tough, right? So what you will need to do, you will need to decompose it. Okay, what app actually consists of? What is that? It’s a…

655 01:22:32.480 –> 01:22:33.420 Ivan Bunin: Cold.

656 01:22:34.290 –> 01:22:36.060 Ivan Bunin: It’s a brand.

657 01:22:37.640 –> 01:22:45.690 Ivan Bunin: It’s, Idea by itself, like, to, to have this, like, the right way, it’s, features.

658 01:22:47.840 –> 01:22:50.390 Ivan Bunin: That will have its marketing.

659 01:22:53.580 –> 01:23:00.119 Ivan Bunin: Okay, but it’s still a lot. If you ask about that, it’s still a ton, like, I cannot just do that.

660 01:23:00.410 –> 01:23:07.889 Ivan Bunin: So then you go further, code, okay. I need to understand what language to use.

661 01:23:08.790 –> 01:23:11.709 Ivan Bunin: I need to do it per device.

662 01:23:13.750 –> 01:23:15.419 Ivan Bunin: I need to optimize it.

663 01:23:17.330 –> 01:23:20.170 Ivan Bunin: Brand. For brand, I need a logo.

664 01:23:21.480 –> 01:23:24.210 Ivan Bunin: I need, let’s say, colors.

665 01:23:24.440 –> 01:23:26.760 Ivan Bunin: I need voice that we’ll be using.

666 01:23:27.300 –> 01:23:30.499 Ivan Bunin: Idea, I need to do competitor research.

667 01:23:33.130 –> 01:23:34.730 Ivan Bunin: Ria search.

668 01:23:35.330 –> 01:23:39.190 Ivan Bunin: I need to, do the Google Trends.

669 01:23:39.790 –> 01:23:41.620 Ivan Bunin: To verify my idea?

670 01:23:42.350 –> 01:23:46.629 Ivan Bunin: Etc. Features. I need to research the problems.

671 01:23:46.830 –> 01:23:50.000 Ivan Bunin: Research… research… okay, here we go.

672 01:23:50.390 –> 01:23:52.610 Ivan Bunin: I need to,

673 01:23:53.050 –> 01:23:59.389 Ivan Bunin: Test other apps to see what they’re using, etc. Marketing. I need to choose the channels.

674 01:23:59.980 –> 01:24:01.150 Ivan Bunin: You see what I mean?

675 01:24:01.320 –> 01:24:17.250 Ivan Bunin: So now, again, this is kind of… a bit easier, but still kind of hard. And then you go further and further. Oh, okay, language. So I need to understand what we’ll be using for the iOS. In here, for the devices, I need to do a version for the mobile, I need to do a version for the desktop.

676 01:24:18.160 –> 01:24:20.739 Ivan Bunin: I need to optimize it, so check for the speed.

677 01:24:22.180 –> 01:24:23.040 Ivan Bunin: Etcetera.

678 01:24:23.220 –> 01:24:33.730 Ivan Bunin: For the logo, I need, again, examples. So, then you continue breaking it out further, further, further, further, further. Up to when you get the…

679 01:24:34.610 –> 01:24:38.369 Ivan Bunin: Actual size that feels comfortable for you.

902 01:50:57.540 –> 01:51:07.360 Ivan Bunin: What does it mean, one-party consent? It means that you and I are talking right now, at least one of us needs to consent to recording. So, for example, Augusto right now cannot record this.

Media & Learning

Pareto Bootcamp

Pareto Bootcamp

Pareto Talent’s free 10-day live Zoom bootcamp (2 h/day + daily homework) — the training gateway into the pareto-talent talent pool. Instructors: ivan-bunin with Amparo “Ampi” Linares and guest team members.

How it works

  • Final project announced day 10 — the same thesis-style project for everyone, never used commercially; it (not attendance) decides graduation. Pass → interview with client success → talent pool → matching with entrepreneurs.
  • Business goal (Ivan): train people (philanthropy) + recruitment pipeline for client placements.
  • Funnel (BC7): 7,000+ applications → ~885 approved → ~800 live. Prior cohort: 10,000 → 700 accepted → 247 finished → 118 accepted. Lifetime: 35,000+ applicants, 2,000+ finishes, ~350 accepted into Pareto.

Tools

Claude

Claude

The LLM pareto-talent (and ivan-bunin) married — “one tool, go deep” instead of chasing every new model.

  • Claude Chat — free tier; dictation built in (Cmd+D / mic icon).
  • Claude Code (paid) — where the real work happens: projects grounded in markdown context (a second brain), agentic routines scheduled by time or webhook, scraping, file processing — replaces n8n-style glue tools.
  • Usage pattern per the bootcamp: feed context (transcripts, Drive files, scraped pages, whole email threads) → short prompts; or have Claude interview you (20 questions) to generate one-pagers that become permanent context.

Appears in: day2-notes · pareto-bootcamp

Tools

Shortwave

Shortwave

Gmail client recommended by ivan-bunin for all executive assistants (free plan covers the essentials). It’s a view over the Gmail account — connect AI tools to Gmail, not to Shortwave.

Key features: to-do grouping of emails with context notes · built-in AI chat (sort the inbox, draft replies in your voice, schedule from your calendar, contextual search) · unsubscribe suggestions · multiple inboxes in one place (yours + entrepreneur’s + personal) · bulk actions for inbox zero.

Appears in: day9-notes

Projects

Competitor Lead Magnet Teardowns

Competitor Lead Magnet Teardowns

Four competitors from Pareto’s space in the VA/hiring space, verified on their live sites, plus their live Meta ad campaigns pulled from the Ad Library (checked Oct 2026). Pattern synthesis at the bottom. The paid-ads layer has its own deeper sweep in competitor-meta-ads.

1. Athena — “Delegation Assessment” quiz

  • Format: 10-question multiple-choice quiz, gated at the end (email only). Site: athena.com/delegation-assessment.
  • Promise: “How well do you actually delegate?” — get your named delegation level, “described plainly,” your specific barrier, and what the next level looks like.
  • Who it’s for: Founders/execs overwhelmed by admin, including skeptics who doubt an EA is worth paying for.
  • Capture & qualify: Email is the only field, requested at the END (“Where should we send your result”) — answers first, paywall second, so completion rates stay high. It qualifies by scoring: answers map to six levels (Beginner → Novice → Intermediate → Advanced → Expert → Mastery).
  • Right after opt-in: Instant results page with personalized diagnosis copy. The bridge to sales is the diagnosis itself: the top three results all tell you “the ceiling here is not your mindset. It is the match.” — i.e., you delegate well, your hire is the problem — then CTA into “Find your EA match” (signup flow, not a calendar).
  • Steal: The diagnosis-to-match bridge. A quiz that flatters high scorers AND converts them, because the punchline is that only a better hire unlocks the next level. Maps to magnet idea #1 in lead-magnet-ideas.
  • Not on Meta: zero ads found in the Ad Library under “athena”/”athena.com” (US-filtered) — Athena grows on SEO, podcasts and PR, not paid social. See competitor-meta-ads.

2. Belay — “Find your MVP” guide (+ resource library)

  • Format: Gated PDF guide on the main site; bigger ungated library (blog, podcast, courses) behind resources.belaysolutions.com.
  • Promise: Behind-the-scenes on the contractors who power Belay — plus the trust stat: “Only 3% of applicants ever become BELAY contractors.”
  • Who it’s for: Leaders comparing providers, who want proof of talent quality before talking to sales.
  • Capture & qualify: Highest-friction of the three — the form asks for a mobile phone number with an SMS-consent checkbox (“automated promotional messages”). That trades volume for intent: anyone who surrenders a phone number is far down the buying path. The “3% of applicants” stat does the qualifying belief-work (top-tier talent, justifying premium pricing).
  • Right after opt-in: “Access the Resource” → guide download, then SMS/email nurture. No calendar forced; the phone number hands sales a direct channel.
  • Steal: Exclusivity stats as belief-building — Pareto already has a better one (“1 in 1,000 applicants”). Put it on every magnet’s delivery page, not just the homepage.
  • On Facebook: surprise — BELAY is the heaviest advertiser in the set (~96 active ads). The ads reveal magnets the site hides: a church campaign, a financial-advisor campaign with a vertical-specific “Financial Advisor’s Delegation Guide,” and a Donald Miller ad that captures leads from comments (“Comment BELAY below and I’ll send you…”). Full sweep in competitor-meta-ads.

3. Virtual Latinos — “Are you doing too much?” quiz + recruiter-call flow

  • Format: Site-wide footer quiz (“Take our quiz — no pressure, just real insights to help you work smarter, not harder”) feeding a short business survey, then a recruiter call. Pricing public on site: Starter $1.6–2.9K/mo, Professional $1.7–3.4K, Advanced $2.1–4.4K. Only 5% of applicants accepted.
  • Who it’s for: US businesses hiring LatAm talent — but organized by vertical: Administrative, Sales & Marketing, Finance & HR, and “Specialized industry” (Legal Assistant, Real Estate Assistant, Medical Assistant, Property Manager).
  • Capture & qualify: Quiz → “register your business” survey (company, needs) → recruitment experts meet with you → they present 3–4 candidates to interview. Nearly the same mechanics as Pareto’s Matching Call, but the verticals act as a self-qualification layer: a lawyer landing on the Legal Assistant page self-sorts before any form.
  • Right after opt-in: Their testimonials show the nurture story — “I was relying previously on an answering service… I finally hired a VL assistant in April 2024… my business has grown by at least 20%” (Planzer Law LLC); “Ileana handles all my calls and keeps me updated on the cases… She also helps me with a lot of the forms” (Shankar & Associates PC, a law firm).
  • Steal: Verticals. VL sells to lawyers with lawyer proof. Pareto’s site sells to “founders” generically — see icp-founder-personas for why law firms are the strongest vertical to attack first.

Virtual Latinos on Facebook — live ads (Ad Library, checked 2026-10-06)

Their organic page is login-walled, but the Meta Ad Library is public — and it’s where the real intel is:

  • Fresh burst, heavy spend: nearly every active ad started Oct 1–5, 2026, with many duplicate IDs of the same creative (“2 ads use this creative and text”). That cadence = an active testing budget, not a brand page run by an intern.
  • Three angles, all aimed at the overwhelmed owner: 1. Trust/partnership (the workhorse, endlessly duplicated): “Trust in someone like you… More than employees, they’re your partners in success. 🤝 Real help for your work and your life.” 2. Weekend pain: “Still working weekends? 😮‍💨 A VA can help you reclaim your time. Hire smart & breathe again.” 3. Task pain: “Still doing everything yourself? ⏰ Get skilled Virtual Professionals to take repetitive tasks off your plate, so you can focus on growing your business.”
  • All image ads, no video in the current rotation. The ads sell the feeling; the quiz on the site does the qualifying. Clever division of labor.
  • The gap: every VL ad is generic — no vertical, no numbers, no offer beyond “get a VA.” Compare with Remote Latinos below, which runs pain-math × vertical × risk reversal. VL is outspending but not out-messaging; that’s Pareto’s opening.

4. Remote Latinos — ads-as-magnet, dual-sided engine

  • Format: No classic gated magnet — the ads are the magnet. Employer side: long-form Facebook ads signed by founder “Esteban” → “Schedule a demo” call. Homepage (remotelatinos.com) mixes self-serve browsing (post jobs, review profiles, free registration) with a done-for-you tier (“Hire Elite Talent”, 30-day warranty, 26-week free replacement guarantee). No public pricing page (404s) — the price anchor lives inside the ads: “roles start at $5/hour.”
  • Promise: Risk reversal cranked to the ceiling: “We will place an appointment setter VA or executive assistant from A-players inside your business and if they don’t perform — IT’S FREE.” Plus niche authority: “the biggest [fractional recruiting firm] in the [REI] space,” “helped over 300 companies in the past 12 months,” and a founder story — first hire was a Colombian VA at GoHighLevel, scaled 30 → 2,000+.
  • Who it’s for: Vertical-first, in the ad copy itself: real estate investors (lead managers, acquisitions, dispo — with name-drops of Ryan Pineda, subto, astro flipping students = audience targeting by affinity), home services (Re-Bath, Five Star Painting, roofing/construction), agencies, law firms, doctors, insurance — and since Oct 5, 2026, a dedicated dental campaign.
  • Capture & qualify: The ad copy does the qualifying — vertical call-outs and pain math filter who raises their hand before any form exists. Capture = the demo call. Their second ad engine makes the promise keepable: talent-side ads run in LATAM (“Fluent in English? It’s time to go global — without leaving home,” “up to $2,000 USD/month,” B2 English required) so the candidate pool is pre-built and employers “meet candidates in under a week.”
  • Right after opt-in: Demo call → matched candidates → warranty-backed placement. Speed and zero-risk are the nurture story, not content.
  • Steal: Their Oct 5 dental ad is the best ad in the category right now: “Your chair earns $300 an hour. Today it sat empty for two of them… Two empty hours a day is $150,000 a year. That’s not a marketing problem. It’s a callback problem.” — pain math × one vertical × one role as the fix (“patient coordinator whose entire job is your schedule: call the recall list, confirm tomorrow’s visits, fill the cancellations”), capped with “Top 1% of over 5,000 candidates… up to 70% less than a US employee.” That is the exact template for Pareto’s law-firm campaign: swap the chair for the billable hour, callbacks for intake calls, coordinator for legal assistant (see icp-founder-personas law ★). Second steal: the dual-sided engine — recruiting candidates with paid ads is what lets you promise speed; it’s a moat, not a cost.

Honorable mention — Wing (demo-as-magnet)

Wing’s magnet is the “free trial, no credit card required” framing — but it’s a managed service ($699–$2,999/mo, live in 72 hours, month-to-month), so the real offer is a demo call. Lesson: when the product is a matched human, the call IS the trial. Pareto’s Matching Guarantee (“meet the top 3, walk away owing nothing”) is the same move, better named.

On Meta, Wing is the attack advertiser: ~92 active ads, vertical pain-math (real estate response time, healthcare admin costs, nonprofit’s “four job titles, one salary”) and conquest ads that name Athena directly (“Before you sign a 90-day minimum… $1,999 a month, cancel anytime, starts in under 48 hours”). Details in competitor-meta-ads.

Synthesis — what the space does

  1. The quiz is the category’s default magnet (Athena and VL both). It filters, scores, and writes the sales pitch into the diagnosis. Pareto has no quiz — this is the gap to fill first (lead-magnet-ideas #1).
  2. Email-only, gate-at-the-end beats form-first (Athena) — except Belay, which happily trades volume for phone-qualified leads. Pick per funnel stage: quiz for top, scorecard+phone for bottom.
  3. Every magnet doubles as a qualifier — levels, exclusivity stats (3%, 5%, 1-in-1,000), fit criteria. Nothing is “just a download.”
  4. Vertical proof converts: VL runs whole verticals with testimonials from that vertical (law firms get law-firm quotes). Pareto’s Wall of Love is horizontal (agency, real estate, content founders) — vertical landing pages are the expansion move.
  5. The paid-ads gap is real: VL buys reach with vibes (“still working weekends?”), Remote Latinos buys it with pain math × vertical × risk reversal (“your chair earns $300 an hour”). Nobody in the set runs an ad pointed at a named diagnostic next step for a named vertical. Pareto’s version: a law-firm pain-math ad → the quiz/scorecard → Matching Call.
  6. Two games, one brand: Remote Latinos recruits candidates with ads in LATAM while recruiting clients with ads in the US. The candidate-recruitment side is what funds their speed promise (“candidates in under a week”) — worth copying before promising speed.

Sources: athena.com/delegation-assessment · belaysolutions.com · virtuallatinos.com · remotelatinos.com · VL Ad Library · RL Ad Library

Competitor Meta Ads

Competitor Meta Ads Sweep

What the VA/hiring space pays to put in front of people. Pulled from the public Meta Ad Library (no login needed) on 2026-10-06. Companion to competitor-lead-magnet-teardowns — that file covers the site funnels, this one covers the paid layer.

Scoreboard

Competitor Meta ads? What they run
BELAY Yes — ~96 results, most active Vertical campaigns (churches, financial advisors, sales teams) + free guides + influencer ads
Wing Yes — ~92 results, most active Vertical pain-math (healthcare, real estate, nonprofit) + competitor-conquest ads
Virtual Latinos Yes — fresh burst Oct 1–5, 2026 Vibes: weekend pain, task pain, trust
Remote Latinos Yes — sustained since Apr 2026 Vertical pain-math + risk reversal + talent-side LATAM ads
Athena No — zero found Nothing under “athena” / “athena.com” even US-filtered; their channel is SEO/podcast/PR
Near No — nothing relevant Keyword matches are unrelated brands

Read: paid social is contested by exactly four players, and the two US-based giants (BELAY, Wing) are the heaviest spenders. Athena spends $0 here and still owns category mindshare — paid social isn’t the only game, but everyone who plays it runs verticals.

BELAY — the quiet giant of paid social

Continuous spend (ads running Jul → Oct 2026), and the most sophisticated operation in the set:

  • Church vertical, full creative set — not a copy-swap, a whole campaign: “Church books aren’t business finances”, “From weekly offerings to annual reporting, church finances follow their own rulebook”, “Pastors, stop booking your own travel and answering endless emails… Get back to your ministry.” They sell EA + bookkeeping to churches as a category of one.
  • Financial advisor vertical, their biggest cluster — with a vertical-specific lead magnet in the ad: “The Financial Advisor’s Delegation Guide.” Copy: “You’re overwhelmed because you’re over-involved. Every approval, every follow up, every small decision routes through you… The client on the other end doesn’t see a busy advisor. They see a slow response.” Plus: “Handing off a task is easy. Getting it back done right is where most advisors give up… nobody has defined what finished looks like.” Also “Stop Paying Six Figures For $20 Tasks” (sales-ops guide) and advisor-testimonial video ads (Steven Jarvis).
  • Sales vertical: “Your best closer is stuck doing admin.” “Not hitting quota? It probably isn’t your sales team. It’s your sales operations.”
  • Influencer-voiced ads + comment capture: Donald Miller (StoryBrand) runs ads for them — “A virtual assistant could increase your productivity by 300% — Comment BELAY below and I’ll send you the information.” Comment-to-DM funnel → resources.belaysolutions.com. No form at all.
  • Client-story videos: Donita (coaching business, 3 months behind on invoices, did bookkeeping on her anniversary trip, nearly tripled revenue), Tim (CEO story).
  • Positioning: “U.S.-based” hammered everywhere (anti-offshoring — the mirror image of Pareto/VL/RL), Right-Fit Guarantee, “matched in about a week.”

Wing — the attack advertiser

  • Competitor-conquest ads, by name (many duplicates, running since Sep 11–21, 2026): “Are you considering Athena or looking to hire an Executive Assistant? Before you sign a 90-day minimum, look at the other column. $1,999 a month. Cancel anytime. EA starts in under 48 hours.” They intercept Athena’s brand search on Meta — the space attacks directly.
  • Real estate pain-math: “Most agents don’t lose listings on price. They lose them on response time.” And a per-file-fee attack on transaction coordinators: “$500-a-file fees add up… Close five deals and you’ve quietly handed over $2,500.”
  • Healthcare vertical with numbers: HIPAA-trained VAs, “Cut Admin Costs By 80%”, patient follow-up (“Stop letting it slip”), intake-call pain.
  • Nonprofit: “Fundraiser. Grant writer. Volunteer coordinator. Executive director. Four job titles, one person, one salary.”
  • Dual-sided engine: “Wing PH Recruitment” ads hire Philippine VAs with full job specs (PHP 25–30K/month) — same move as Remote Latinos: the candidate pool is built with paid ads.

Virtual Latinos & Remote Latinos

Covered in detail in competitor-lead-magnet-teardowns (VL section + RL teardown). Short version: VL buys reach with vibes (“Still working weekends? 😮‍💨”), RL buys it with pain-math × vertical × risk reversal (the Oct 5 dental ad: “$150,000 a year in empty chair time… that’s not a marketing problem, it’s a callback problem”). RL also runs the talent-side LATAM ads (“up to $2,000 USD/month”) that fund their “candidates in under a week” promise.

Patterns Pareto can use

  1. Verticals are table stakes; depth is the differentiator. Everyone name-drops a vertical in copy. BELAY builds a whole creative set for one vertical (churches) including a vertical-specific guide. That’s the gap between “targeting lawyers” and “selling to lawyers.”
  2. Ads don’t have to sell the call. BELAY’s biggest vertical campaign gives away a guide (Delegation Guide for advisors) — top-of-funnel ad → nurture → call. Pareto’s equivalent: a law-firm delegation/scorecard asset as the ad destination, Matching Call as the back end.
  3. Conquest ads are live in this space. Wing attacks Athena by name and price ($1,999 cancel-anytime vs “90-day minimum”). An aggressive flank is available (e.g., vs the $3,000/mo incumbents) — but it’s a knife that cuts both ways on trust.
  4. Numbers beat vibes. Wing’s “80% / 3-minute response / $2,500 handed over”, RL’s “$150k/yr chair math” — every concrete ad has a number in it. VL’s numberless ads are the counterexample of what not to run.
  5. The influencer + comment-to-DM funnel is unclaimed. BELAY × Donald Miller is exactly the shape of a Kasim-aslam ad (“comment PARETO and I’ll send you…”) — and Kasim already co-owns the brand’s story (kasim-aslam).
  6. The US-based vs LatAm line is drawn. BELAY hammers “U.S.-based” as the trust play; VL/RL sell the same trust through “bilingual, college-educated, top 1%.” Pareto needs its own one-line answer to “why LatAm, why not BELAY” on every ad destination.

Refresh

Rerun these Ad Library searches monthly (public, no login): belaysolutions · wingassistant · virtuallatinos · remotelatinos. Athena and Near stay on the watchlist but showed nothing under their keywords on 2026-10-06.

Icp Founder Personas

ICP & Founder Personas (by cause, in client words)

Companion to competitor-lead-magnet-teardowns and lead-magnet-ideas. Quotes from wall-of-love unless noted; law persona flagged where evidence is hypothesis, not proof.

The ICP (company-level filter)

US-based founder of a 7–8-figure service business, doing $1M+/yr, who is personally the operational bottleneck of the company and can pay $3,000/mo + $3,000 placement without flinching.

  • Firm gates: US-based · founder-led (they ARE the ops department) · revenue high enough that 10 reclaimed hrs/week at their rate dwarfs $36k/yr
  • Psychographic gates: wants a strategic full-time partner, not a task-list VA · AI-open (the “AI-Powered Right Hand” pitch lands) · values loyalty and long-term placement over cheap churn-and-burn
  • Disqualifiers: businesses under ~$250k revenue · “I need 5 hours a week of data entry” · offshore-bargain hunters · anyone wanting round-the-clock coverage (one full-time right hand, one timezone)
  • The wedge (from the site’s own numbers): 60%+ of incoming founders were burned by a previous VA. See the “Burned before” overlay below.

Persona 1 — “Everyone bills time except me” (Agency Owner at Capacity)

  • Cause: client communication, account management and scheduling eat the founder’s calendar; delivery stops scaling; the agency can’t take client #12.
  • In their words: “I just can’t even imagine not having my EA right now. I can’t fathom a world where she’s not a big part of it” (Joe Polish, Genius Network). “A beast. She’s on it. She’s super efficient and a master task manager” (Marie Monet). “Huge help… I keep referring all of my people to you” (Nick Foster).
  • What they’ve tried: another PM tool, a part-time freelancer, promoting a junior account manager into burnout.
  • Trigger event: dropped balls on a big account, or a health/burnout scare.
  • Where they are: agency masterminds, agency podcasts, Genius Network-style peer groups.
  • Magnets that fit: quiz #1 (“Should You Hire a Right Hand?”) · VA-vs-Right-Hand scorecard #4 · 7 Laws of Delegation one-pager #6.

Persona 2 — “The deal dies in my inbox” (Real Estate / Investor Operator)

  • Cause: transaction coordination, listing admin, and follow-up are time-critical; every slow reply is money on the table; deal flow lives in a chaotic inbox.
  • In their words: Jon Vroman tells the story of his EA taking over his Zillow listings hunt. “My executive assistant runs point on critical projects and keeps track of so many endless opportunities” (Andrew Myers). “Always punctual, reliable, and fully prepared… someone I can trust without hesitation” (Kevin Whatley).
  • What they’ve tried: transaction coordinators per deal, ISA cold callers, showing assistants — all task-shaped, none strategic.
  • Trigger event: a deal lost to slow follow-up; portfolio crosses ~10 doors/properties and admin doubles.
  • Where they are: real estate investor communities, RE podcasts, Zillow/BiggerPockets world.
  • Magnets that fit: ROI calculator #2 · hiring-regions benchmarks report #12 (what a coordinator costs where).

Persona 3 — “If I don’t post it, it doesn’t exist” (Creator / Coach with a Content Bottleneck)

  • Cause: production, publishing, DMs and launch ops pile on top of actually making content; the channel goes quiet every launch.
  • In their words: “I got him his own Canva account, and he went and made 100 social posts for Instagram… really good initiative” (Chris Thompson). “I won’t even tell her to do it, and she’ll just go and figure out how to do it” (Elina Panteleyeva).
  • What they’ve tried: video editors and VAs who need frame-by-frame instructions — initiative never shows up.
  • Trigger event: a launch where ops crushed creation, or a 2-week silence on the channel.
  • Where they are: creator economy newsletters, YouTube, Skool communities.
  • Magnets that fit: 7-tool AI stack kit #10 · “Context over prompts” email course #11.

Persona 4 — “I bill $400 an hour and I’m chasing file names” (Law Firm Owner) ★ Fran’s pick

  • Cause: intake calls, case-status updates, forms/filings, rescheduling — high-value professional time burned on $20/hr work; answering services lose clients.
  • Evidence this vertical is real (competitor proof): Virtual Latinos runs an entire Legal Assistant vertical, and their law-firm clients say it plainly — “Ileana handles all my calls and keeps me updated on the cases… She also helps me with a lot of the forms” (Shankar & Associates PC); “I was relying previously on an answering service… my business has grown by at least 20%” (Planzer Law LLC, who then promoted their VL receptionist to legal assistant).
  • In their words (hypothesis persona — constructed, not yet sourced from Pareto’s wall): “Every missed call is a case walking to another firm. My paralegal quit in June. I’m doing intake between depositions.” Flag: no lawyer testimonial exists on wall-of-love yet — that’s whitespace, not disproof.
  • Why it’s the strongest ROI story in the book: 10 hrs/week back at a $300–500 billed rate = $150–250k/yr recovered, against $36k+fee. No other persona’s math comes close.
  • Watch-outs: confidentiality/NDA and conflicts handling need a standard answer; “assistant” not “paralegal” (no legal advice scope).
  • Magnets that fit (verticalized): “Is your firm running you?” scorecard (scorecard #4, legal edition) · legal-assistant salary benchmarks #12 · legal job-posting swipe file #8.
  • Validation next step: ask the Pareto team (Gala owns client acquisition) whether any placed founders are in legal; if yes, hunt their Wall-of-Love quote; if no, the VL testimonials prove demand — Pareto would be entering with the 1-in-1,000 quality bar VL doesn’t have.

Overlay — “Burned before” (the cross-persona qualifier)

“I’ve had three different executive assistants before, and I thought it was me… I was burning through them. They just weren’t up to the task” (Eric Ritter, matched to Agustina). This isn’t a fourth persona — it’s the emotional state most leads arrive in (the site says 60%+). Every magnet should speak to it: the scorecard names the failure, the Matching Guarantee and lifetime replacement are the antidote, the 93%-at-12-months stat is the proof.

Next steps

  1. Build quiz #1 + scorecard #4 (GHL-native) — they serve every persona.
  2. Test ONE vertical landing page: legal (strongest math, proven demand via VL).
  3. Mine the full Wall of Love video titles for vertical counts (how many agency/RE/legal clients exist today).
  4. Validation interviews: 2–3 real clients per persona; replace the hypothesis quote in Persona 4 with a real one.

Projects

Lead Magnet Ideas

Lead Magnet Ideas

Free assets to capture leads, each grounded in something this vault already documents. Audience: F = founder side (goal: Matching Call), E = EA side (goal: bootcamp application). Types marked GHL can be built natively in GoHighLevel, like the existing qualified/not-qualified flow.

Quizzes & calculators (GHL-native, highest priority)

  1. “Should You Hire a Right Hand?” scored quiz (F) — 10 yes/no questions from the Structural Trap stats (80% drowning in admin, 70% no time, 60%+ burned by a VA). Score → qualified/not-qualified page → calendar. Source: pareto-talent-website.
  2. Founder Time & Money ROI calculator (F) — hours/week on admin × founder hourly rate = annual loss, vs the $3k/mo price. The site’s 12.5 hrs/week × $200/hr = 4.3x return math, made interactive. Source: pareto-talent-website.
  3. “Could You Pass the Bootcamp?” self-check (E) — the published fit criteria (2+ yrs experience, English, Slack/ClickUp, 2 h/day commitment) as a scored checklist that funnels straight into the quick application. Source: bootcamp-website.

Checklists & one-pagers (PDF, fastest to ship)

  1. “The VA vs a Right Hand” scorecard (F) — rate your current assistant on the behaviors from the site’s comparison table (waits vs anticipates, excuses vs owns it, stops vs closes loops). Doubles as a qualifier for switching. Source: pareto-talent-website, jargon.
  2. 30 things to delegate in your first 30 days (F) — listicle PDF seeded from the founder stats and the delegation ladder (Delegator → Strategist → Visionary). Source: pareto-talent-website.
  3. The 7 Laws of Delegation one-pager (F) — condensed from the Delegation Mastermind component and Kasim’s Seven Laws video series. Source: pareto-talent-website, kasim-aslam.
  4. Inbox zero + calendar Tetris checklist (E) — Day 9 core skills as a printable. Source: pareto-bootcamp day 9, shortwave.

Swipe files & templates

  1. Job posting swipe file (F) — “steal the exact structure” — condensation of HIRE Step 2 + the free templates at thehirebook.com/free, for founders who won’t read the book. Source: the-hire-book, step-2-create-a-job-posting.
  2. Founder’s Second Brain starter template (F, differentiated) — a stripped Obsidian/Notion vault with SOP, vendor and meeting-note skeletons. Pareto literally sells “Second Brain OS” as an offer component — give a taste away. Source: pareto-talent-website, this whole vault.
  3. “The exact 7-tool AI stack” kit (E+F) — Claude, ChatGPT, Canva, CapCut, N8N, Lovable, Operator AI + what each one does for the founder. Very 2026, very shareable. Source: pareto-talent-website, claude.

Email mini-courses

  1. “Context over prompts” 5-day course (F+E) — one Ivan teaching per day (context engineering, marrying one tool, dictation, second brains, closing loops), each ending with the CTA. Source: ivan-bunin, pareto-bootcamp day 2.
  2. “What EAs really cost” benchmarks report (F) — salary + policy data across the 6 hiring regions (starts at $1k/mo LATAM, PH at $1.5k, 20-day PTO norms). Data magnets get linked. Source: hiring-regions, pareto-talent.

How to pick first

Start with 1 or 2 (quiz) + 4 (scorecard): both GHL-native, reuse the existing calendar embed and qualified/not-qualified plumbing, and qualify leads instead of just collecting emails. Ship one PDF (4 or 6) as the delivery artifact after the form.

Rules from the vault itself

  • Magnets should filter, not just attract — the whole Pareto system is filter-before-interview (pareto-talent-framework). A quiz that disqualifies is on-brand.
  • Proof closes: every delivery page gets one wall-of-love testimonial matched by tenure (30/90/365 days).
  • Free book is the top of their funnel — don’t compete with thehirebook.com/free; complement it (scorecard, calculator, swipe file).
